Hon. gentlemen must not forget that the Government is building a railway to Hudson bay and this agreement gives the Canadian Northern and its subsidiary companies the right to operate the Hudson Bay railway. That I am not objecting to at all.
'But,' says the hon. gentleman from St. John, 'if it were only within the control of the Governor in Council :I would be satisfied; I have faith,' he says, 'in the Governor in Council in this regard, but I have no faith in the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.' Well, the Railway Commission of Canada is likely in my judgment, to protect the interests of this country in any running rights agreement, but it is only very recently that the hon. member for :St. John has developed such confidence in the Governor in Council. It is not so long ago, when he was speaking on the question of the increase of capital of the subsidiary companies in the Canadian Northern Railway system, that he thought it was worth while to hold this House of Commons for half a day in order, that he might endeavour to convince us that it was not proper to confide to the Governor in Council the mere power to approve of an increase of capitalization of a subsidiary company.	He
thought he should delay the House for half

a day to show that the Governor in Council was not fit to decide a matter of such responsibility as to approve of an increase in capitalization of a subsidiary company, allowing it was but a part of a great company whose capitalization could not be increased. A few days passed, and then the hon. member came down with an amendment of his own, and he was going to lock up all the stock of this company into a thirty million dollar pocket, then he was going to put it in trust in the name of the Receiver General for Canada, and then he was going to let Mackenzie and Mann take the responsibility of running the road, and if they did not make a success of it lose it, but if they did make a success, they had to give it over to the country on an arbitrated value not greater than thirty million dollars. And he added a clause to his resolution saying that in the meantime Mackenzie and Mann should be left in charge of the Canadian Northern system. One day went by, and the hon. member told the House that he had decided to eliminate that last clause after due consideration; he had decided that it would be better not to insist on Mackenzie and Mann running the road instead of the Government. The hon. member had looked up the speech of the hon. ex-Minister of Railways, and he saw that that hon. gentleman held the directly opposite stage on the question, and consequently he struck a compromise, and he said he was ready to leave it to the Governor in Council to decide, whether the Government would run the Canadian Northern in the meantime or whether Mackenzie and Mann would run it.
The attitude of the hon. member for St. John is this:	That though the Governor
in Council is not a body to be trusted with the increase of capitalization of a subsidiary company, it is to be trusted to decide of its own motion without the authority of the Parliament of Canada, whether this country shall assume a debt of $360,000,000 and operate a railway of 10,000 miles. What a great body this Governor in Council must be in the eyes of the hon. member for St. John- it is quite competent to decide on the largest commercial question that has ever faced this country without the authority of Parliament at all, but it is utterly incompetent to be trusted to approve of the increase of capitalization of a small subsidiary company.

John (Mr. Pugsley) in that he has taken one clause out of about three which were left in the resolution moved by

But I submit that the leader of the Opposition has not done very much justice to the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux).
The hon. member for Rouville had a policy also, and 1 cannot see any of it summarized in this grand total moved to-day by the leader of the Opposition. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) wanted to delay the issue six months notwithstanding that the Minister of Railways in the Government he supported declared that we could not afford to delay at all, six months was about the time he thought we should lie 'back and do nothing. The hon. member for Middlesex (Mr. Ross) thought we had better wait until next session and then start a commission of expert accountants from amongst the members of this House of Commons to find out all about the finances and business of the Canadian Northern railway. But the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Leinieux) was not satisfied with any of the propositions made by his friends, and he declared in the House that we should not make a move at any time, but should leave everything go to rack and ruin until we had a general election. Now, I would like to ask the leader of the Opposition how he is going to 'summarize' this sentence of his lieutenant from Rouville, taken with the sentence I have quoted from the hon. member for South Renfrew, as to going ahead at once with the road. Here is what the hon. member for Rouville said:
Sir, this policy means the completion of a third transcontinental railway, and I say that the Government has no mandate to commit the country to the immediate completion of that third transcontinental railway.
He says we have no mandate whatever to complete this road. It would be interesting indeed to hear the right hon. gentleman 'summarize' that statement with the statement I have just quoted from the hon. member for South Renfrew. The hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) went on:

I say that pending the Redistribution Bill, the Government cannot consistently commit the new electorate to that huge guarantee. The new constituencies have the right to be heard from in reference to the new venture. We cannot and we must not saddle the new electorate with this guarantee of $45,000,000 without the consent of that new electorate.
He was asked by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) whether he would defer everything until after the next election, to w'hieh he answered, yes.

Here is the question and the answer:
Mr. Edwards: Would the gentleman argue that action should be deferred until after the next election?
Mr. Lemieux: Yes, and the people will then condemn the action of the Government.
I wanted to have that little rider added to the 'yes.'

Very well, but it only emphasizes the affirmative 'yes.' Will the hon. gentleman tell me this: How is an hon. member of this House, who declares that we should not 'commit the country to a guarantee at all, that we should not move a step until after the next general election, going to vote now for an amendment which means that we commit the country to me whole $45,000,000 and take an option in lieu thereof^ I have no doubt the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) is going to vote for this amendment; he belongs now to the 'vote for everything' party, and he can change as quickly as a moving-picture show or as any other of the changing scenes of life.
The hon. member for St. John is in the most remarkable position of all. He declared that we could not take this step without putting all the stock of the company into a trust fund in the hands of the Receiver-General for Canada. The leader of the Opposition thinks it is just as well outstanding; but the hon. member for St. John thinks we had better gather it in now and leave it in trust in the hands of the Receiver General of Canada, take from Mackenzie and Mann their lands, stocks, townsites and services, and then give them a chance to keep the road going, to make the system pay, to dispose of all this $45,000,000; and if they succeed, we shall take the road from them at a fraction of its value, and if they do not succeed, we shall take the road from them without giving them anything at all, and he is surprised and astonished a the very
suggestion that Mackenzie and Mann would not grasp at such a great opportunity as that.
In the discussion of this subject I venture to suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that, in their hurry to get hold of something that will appeal with a dulcet sound to the electorate of Canada, knowing as they do that it is not an easy matter for an elector, with the time at his disposal, to grasp even the salient facts of an intricate problem of this kind, they have forgotten their responsibilities as members of this House; they have forgotten that we are engaged in the solution of a very vast, intricate and difficult problem, on the proper solution of which depends in large degree the prosperity of this country. It is true that Parliament is master of the situation to this extent, that, if it is not able to make an arrangement with the owners of this stock and of this road, then it can refuse the grant and let liquidation follow. Liquidation will follow, just as it would have followed the Grand Trunk Pacific in 1909, if the loan that the hon. gentlemen supported had not been made, because the Grand Trunk Pacific in their letter stated that that would be the result, if the loan were not made. We have arrived at this stage m the case of the Canadian Northern that, unless assistance is given, the road will pursue the course inevitable. It will find itself unable to link up and get into a paying position; it will find itself unable to maintain outlying lines, which so isolated cannot {pay, consequently. If we cannot come to terms witli these gentlemen we have only one alternative: We have to do nothing and let a receivership follow as quickly as it will. We cannot disguise [DOT]that fact as serious members of Parliament. We have two choices and only two, namely:	To make an arrangement
with Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, the holders of this stock; or il we cannot make such an arrangement, then the other alternative is: Let the road go into liquidation. Therefore, we have to deal with them, to come to the best terms we can and then say: Are these, the best terms we can procure, better than the other alternative ? If the best terms we are able to secure are better than the other alternative, the duty of this House, in justice to the people we represent, is to accept these terms. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) says that we are legislators. He forgets that not only are we legislators, but we are negotiators. We

are parties to a bargain; we necessarily must be parties to a bargain unless we are prepared to see liquidation come. We are legislators; but we are first of all negotiators; and it is beyond the power of this Parliament, except by negotiation, to put shape to what the hon. member for St. John and the leader of the Opposition say is their policy, namely: To reduce the capital stock to $30,000,000. This Parliament has no power under the authority granted by the British North America Act to interfere with property and civil rights in this country. Only by the consent of the stockholders can that be done; and only by the consent of the stockholders can any of these things be effected which have been effected and which have been enacted under the arrangement we now propose. The Parliament of this country is bound to set itself face to face with the facts and say: Is there any reasonable likelihood that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, would for one moment think of consenting to such an alternative as that represented by the right hon. leader of the Opposition ? * Oh,' says the hon. member for St. John, ' why would they not ?-they have not put a dollar into this road; they have done nothing for this road at all.' I submit this, and I ask hon. gentlemen to ponder over it, that there are three main elements in the consideration that Mackenzie, Mann and Company have given to the Canadian Northern. There are the grants of land which they turned over; there are next the townsites which are now turned in for our security, and there is thirdly the release on the behalf of the Canadian Northern absolutely of their entire claim for their services to this road, for their financing of this road during a period of about eighteen years.
The hon. gentleman says there are grants of land which they turned over. Were not those grants made specifically for the construction of the railway to the railway company?

I address myself to
answering that question, and without boasting, I venture to think that, when I am through the hon. member for St. John will deem that he has been answered.
The grants of land were made and went to those who should construct three railways, namely, the Manitoba and Southeastern, the Winnipeg and Hudson Bay, and the Lake Manitoba Railway and Canal Company's road. The grants of land went with the charters, titles to be made upon construction of the roads; and whoever

acquired the charters and the right to construct the roads, and did construct them, would have earned those land grants. The hon. member for St. John will have no difficulty in following me, because he has passed through the same experience that I am now endeavouring to recite.

Will my hon. friend
allow me to ask another question?
Yes, but I will not forget what I am at.

I will refresh my hon.
friend's memory. Were not the several contracts by the Government to give the land grants made directly between the Crown and the railway companies?

They were made between the Crown and the railway companies. The Crown gave the charters; the land grants followed the charters; and whoever fulfilled the terms of the charters got the land grants. The Lake Manitoba Railway and Canal Company entered into an agreement with the contractors, Mackenzie, Mann and Company, that Mackenzie, Mann and Company would build the railway, and they, having built the railway, would get the land grants. Whoever built the railway would get the land grants. The same thing is true in the case of the Winnipeg and Hudson Bay and in the case of the Manitoba and Southeastern. Mackenzie and Mann earned the land grant, just as fairly as the hon. member for St. John ever earned anything in his life. They got it by a contract with the company by which they built the road. They built the road; the land grant was theirs and they were in a position to sell it, keep it, or do just what they liked with it. They kept 100,000 acres of a land grant of 4,102,000 acres, and the rest of the land grant they turned over to the Canadian Northern Railway Company of Canada. Was the land grant theirs before they turned it over or not? Does the hon. member for St. John say it was not theirs?

What I will say to my hon. friend is this, that my information is that all these roads, for which land grants were given, were constructed with the proceeds of bonds which were issued against the roads which represent the value of the roads; and that those bonds are outstanding to-day. and it was equity and justice that the proceeds of the lands should all go into the railway company.

I am quite as well
aware as the hon. member for St. John that moneys were raised on the road and the roads were encumbered, and the land grants became the property of the men who built the road, having the charter to do it. But my hon. friend's statement was not an answer. My question was, whether or not before these lands were turned over they were the property of Mackenzie and Mann in order to do what they liked with it. I know one hon. member who will not answer that question in the negative in this House.

My belief is that the
proceeds of these lands belong to the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and had there been other shareholders than Mackenzie and Mann the proceeds would have been divided, but Mackenzie and Mann owned the railway company.
The Canadian Northern was formed in 1899. Now, were or were not Mackenzie, Mann and Company in a position to hold or dispose of these land grants they had previously earned just as they might desire?

My hon. friend knows

adian Northern Railway Montreal Land Company, which owns this model city, we should take that interest in and make it the property of the Canadian Northern Railway system. I have never been able to see the value of adding interest to fallacies by repeatedly exposing them. But perhaps an exception may be here allowed. The model city was a real estate speculation near Montreal. Mackenzie, Mann and Company had some interest in it, as I have often stated to the House. A company of brokers financed the enterprise of tunnelling the mountain at Montreal, financed the bonds of the Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company. payment and take a lien for the money we pay out to those who have righteous; demands against the road; let us investigate the proposition fully; let us say to the men who are connected with this enterprise: you should take in other Canadians and other men throughout the empire who have status in the financial world to help you on with this; enterprise, if the Government had placed before the House and the country all the facts in connection with the enterprise, then they might have confidence in asking Parliament and the Canadian people to ratify their policy. But they have not done that. To-day, the Solicitor General actually had the temerity to say that not one item of the report they made with reference to the status of this enterprise, had been challenged or questioned. How could their report in regard to Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited, be questioned or challenged, how could any member of this House, seeing that proper inquiry was excluded by the Government, have access to the documents in the possession of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, to ascertain whether the statements made by the Solicitor General and his colleagues be challenged.
But with evidence verified by an affidavit which would not be received by any court in this country as proof of the fact where it was questioned-and these facts are all questioned-my hon. friend closed his last speech on this measure with the bombastic assurance that not a single item of this report had been questioned, nor a single suggestion made that it was untrue. Under these circumstances, Canada is asked to pass it by; and lest these people go into liquidation, Canada must assume the present load of debt and must go into the vast unknown future of liabilities which will necessarily follow the passage of this measure. Without any care or thought, without any investigation worthy of the name, the Government are committing this country to this position. I am glad to say I believe that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House will, as we have done before during this discussion, proceed to declare that the interests of Canada demand that this measure should not be passed and that it should never become law in this country.

Mr. VERVILLE moved in amendment, seconded by Mr. Carroll:
That the said Bill he not now read a third time but that it be referred to a Committee of the Whole with instruction that they have power to amend the same by providing that the Act shall come into force by proclamation of His Royal Highness the Governor General, which may be issued when Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited, who are the owners of coal mines in the Island of Vancouver, shall have agreed to a board of conciliation, as requested by the operatives of the said mines.
He said: In support of my amendment 1 shall be very brief. In the discussion we had in the House some time ago, and in the return presented to the House, it was admitted that it was almost impossible for the Government to compel Mackenzie, Mann and Company to accept a board of conciliation. It was proved by the return, and in the agreement -at that time, and admitted by the Minister of Labour, that it was impossible to get the opposing parties

together. It was proved, by the return that the men were largely favourable to having a board of conciliation, and it seems to me at the present time that we have the power in our hands, and it is the right time, to force Mackenzie, Mann and Company, who are anxious to receive the guarantee of this amount of money, to accept a board of conciliation. My amendment does not say that the strike should be settled, because I do not believe it is within the jurisdiction of the Government or of this House to say that a strike should be settled. At the same time we should force, whenever we have occasion to do it, those who may be interested to agree to conciliation. I say that, because any one who wants a guarantee of public money should abide by the laws of the country. In the past, we have seen the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific having to accept the awards of boards of conciliation; and I should have the support of the Minister of Labour because I have heard him make such statements in this House time and again, and I know he has forced the Grand Trunk to abide by the decision rendered by a board of conciliation. At this stage, Mr. Speaker, the strike which is still on in Vancouver island, is too costly for. the country. I could not get the amount it has cost the Government, because I had a question on the Order Paper, which has been made an order of the House, and the information has not yet come down; but we can imagine that it has cost probably one quarter or half a million dollars so far to have the militia guarding the mines. It seems to me at the present time it would be a great saving to the country to force the owners to have a conciliation board, so as to enable not only the members of this House but also the public to understand the real situation existing on Vancouver island.
The House will agree with me that my amendment is strictly on conciliation grounds, and I do not see why I should not, and I hope I will, receive the approval of both sides of the House on this question. There is no harm whatever in forcing Mackenzie and Mann to accept a board of conciliation, so as to give an opportunity during the recess of Parliament to find out the exact condition of affairs, because in the return we have had we have seen only one side of the question, and it has been explained in another way by the other side. By this resolution it is particularly stated that this principle not only applies	to the	Canadian
Northern railway, but should apply to every railway company when it makes a demand for assistance. It is outside the jurisdiction of the Government to state plainly that strikes must be settled, because the trouble may come from one side or the other; but we have a law on the statute-books which has worked fairly well in a good many cases, and at the present time I do not see why we should not force Mackenzie and Mann to have a board of conciliation. That is the reason I move this amendment.

Is the hon. member
for Maisonneuve in a position to state that Mackenzie and Mann are the owners of these mines on Vancouver island?

My amendment states
plainly some mines; it does not say all the mines. I am told that Mackenzie and Mann are the owners of some of the mines on Vancouver island.

I cannot say for certain, but I am told that the Canadian Collieries are controlled by Mackenzie and Mann, and until such time as it is proved to the contrary, I will stick to that statement.
If the hon. member is not in a position to state that Mackenzie and Mann have any interest in any mine in Vancouver, I ask if this amendment is in. order?
I think I can state to-the hon. member that Mackenzie and Mann do not control any single mine on Vancouver island.
We had it made plain in the previous discussion that Mackenzie and Mann were the parties to settle that question. The Minister of Labour knows it, and every one who has seen the return knows it.

I think I should say a word or two on this amendment. As I understand the wording of the amendment, two statements in substance are made, or are implied. One is that Mackenzie and Mann own one or more coal mines on Vancouver island, a number of miners connected with which are on strike, and the other is that Mackenzie and Mann's workingmen have requested a board of conciliation. The only mining company on Vancouver island in which Mackenzie and Mann are at all

interested, so far as I am aware, is the Canadian Collieries, Limited. That company operates seven mines at Cumberland, a place about 120 miles north of Victoria, and one mine eight or ten miles south of Nanaimo. I understand that Mackenzie and Mann hold only very limited shares in that company, that they have not the control of any of the mines which I have mentioned and that they are not interested in any other mines on Vancouver island-I am not aware that the workmen ever requested a board of conciliation; on the contrary, they refused a board of conciliation when offered one by the Labour Department. The men went on strike at Cumberland on September 16, 1912, and some two or three days afterwards at their other mines south of Nanaimo, at a place called Extension. The first intimation I had of any labour trouble on Vancouver island was an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of September 19, 1912. Without having any direct notification from the men or from any one else, or without any information whatever except what I saw in the papers, I sent a message to the secretary of the organization at Cumberland, in these words:
Peter McNiven,
Secretary United Mine Workers Lodge, Cumberland, B.C.
My attention has been drawn to newspaper despatches announcing the occurrence of coal miners' strike at Cumberland mines. The Industrial Disputes Investigation Act provides means for possible settlement of all matters in dispute by reference to an impartial board ot three members, on which company and workmen concerned may each have a representative of their own selection. Law does not compel acceptance of board findings but forbids strikes or lockouts pending inquiry under severe penalties. In present case requirements of the Act do not appear to have been satisfied, and I am desirous of learning particulars of dispute by telegram without delay. Department will furnish any fuller explanation of Industrial disputes law which may be required, and is to-day mailing you copies of this law and forms of application thereunder. In the event of proper application being made, everything possible will be done to expedite procedure under Act.
It happened that Peter McNiven, whose name we had on our list of officers of the different unions, had been superseded by a man called McAllister, and the next day I received a message from McAllister as follows:
Hon. T. W. Crothers,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa.
There is no strike declared at Cumberland mines. The company have openly discriminated against men who were taking an active part in union organization. They have also refused

to meet a committee of men. The men decided to take a holiday, after which the company gave orders for men to take their tools out of the mines.
That was the reply to the message that I sent them suggesting that they should apply for a board of conciliation and enclosing copy of the Industrial Disputes Act and blank forms upon which they might make application for the board. The reply which I have read to the House states that there was no strike, but that there was a lockout. The commissioner afterwards appointed by the Government to investigate conditions on Vancouver island found that as a matter of fact these men had gone on strike. They were urged over and over again to ask for a board of conciliation, but they constantly refused to act. I spent several weeks upon the island. I went first to the city of Vancouver, and there met a number of the labour leaders and heard what they had to say in regard to the matter. I then went over to the city of Victoria and saw the Minister of Mines and the officers of his department and the managers of all the coal mines on Vancouver island. I then went to Cumberland and met twenty-seven of the men who were on strike and heard what they had to say about the situation- I had before me forty of the men who were actually working, and of these only one man had any complaint to make; all the others were perfectly satisfied with the conditions in the mines. This one man rose and said: I am not satisfied. I said: What is your grievance? He said:	I am not getting enough
money for the work which I am doing.
I said: How much do you get per diem throughout the year, after paying for your explosives? What is your net income? He said: About $5 a day. At Nanaimo I saw a large number, seventeen, I think, of the men who were on strike, as well as a large number of those who were opposed to the strike. I consulted the mayor of the city of Nanaimo, the police magistrate, members of Parliament and two or three ministers of the gospel. I addressed a meeting there on this question, and I attended a meeting at Ladysmith, which is the water port for the mines at Extension, and addressed some 200 miners. At South Wellington I addressed 120 men. I think that I became acquainted with the views of the men who were in favour of the strike, of the men who were opposed to the strike, of the managers of the different companies and of the owners of the different mines. This amendment, proposed by my

hon. friend the member for Maisonneuve, does not set forth accurately the facts. It says impliedly, if not in so many words, that the miners requested a board of conciliation. This they did not do; on the contrary, they refused a board of conciliation. The mines in which Mackenzie and Mann are interested are but a few of the many coal mines on Vancouver island where strikes occurred simultaneously. How would it do for my hon. friend the member for Maisonneuve to provide in his amendment that the Act shall not be proclaimed until all those interested in the different mines in Vancouver island ask for a board of conciliation and submit to any award that may be made by such board?

This amendment, in my estimation is perfectly useless under the circumstances; and the hon. members who have moved and seconded it know perfectly well that it will be fruitless in every respect. I venture to say that neither one of the hon. gentlemen who have imposed this amendment on the House at this particular time ever approached the Minister of Labour, as Minister of Labour, or asked his assistance in any way to the solution of this difficult problem. Other members from British Columbia and myself have been constantly in touch with the Minister of Labour; we have discussed this question privately in his office, in his official capacity, from every conceivable angle and sacrificed much time and energy, especially the two representatives from that district, in trying to secure a solution of this question. Now hon. gentlemen come forward and introduce an amendment with no other earthly reason than to make a little bit of petty, political capital out of the occasion. There is not a vestige of interest in the heart of either one of these gentlemen to attain a solution of the problem or they would have been spending their time, as men claiming to represent the labour interests of this country in a peculiar manner, in assisting us during the last two or three years to arriye at some solution of the problem. I am prepared now and so are my colleagues to do anything that human power can do to bring about a happy solution of this trouble. We know and hon. gentlemen know that the amendment is simply put before you in order to confuse the whole question and, if possible, make a little political capital. The right hon. gentleman who intends to vote for this amendment knows that perfectly well and he knows he will vote for it with no hope of solving the solution, but simply to make political capital.

When the Bill was under consideration in committee, I said a few w'ords in connection with the unfortunate strike of the coal miners on the island of Vancouver, and I appealed to the Prime Minister, who was in his seat, that something should be done to get Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann to procure a peaceful settlement of the strike which was then and is now in progress in the mines controlled by them in British Columbia. At that time the reason given by the right hon. gentleman who leads the House was that the Bill did not anticipate taking control of the coal mines, nor did it anticipate taking over the coal mines as *security for the $45,000,000 of bond [DOT]guarantee that the Government are giving to Mackenzie and Mann or to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. The *Prime Minister said, however, that he *would take the matter into consideration. I suggested then that if steps were not taken I or some other hon. member would move an amendment to that effect before the Bill received a third reading, and that is in effect the amendment which my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Ver-ville) has brought before the House. An hon. gentleman from British Columbia asked if Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann actually controlled the coal mines in British Columbia. I say they do. I say they control the Canadian Collieries, Limited, in British Columbia. I say they operate coal mines in Cumberland; they operate at least six mines in British Columbia and I do not think there is any gentleman who knows it better than the hon. gentleman who asked the question.
I think I am in a position to know the actual facts as well as any hon. gentleman and the facts which 1 stated are facts.

The hon. gentleman
thinks they are facts. I know that the statements I am making are facts, and all the hon. gentlemen know that too. If the hon. member would read the correspondence brought down by the Minister of Labour and read to the House during the discussion of this unfortunate trouble some months ago, he would see that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann do control and that it was their officials in Toronto who sought

a settlement of this strike through the mediation of the minister.
At one time Mackenzie and Mann controlled some mines; but I say that recently they have not controlled them and they do not control them today.
I happen to be a director of a coal mine on Vancouver island which has suffered immediately through this - strike-

If the hon. gentleman
has anything to say, he can make his speech afterwards.

If Mackenzie and Mann

I submit that only applies to a question within the personal experience of a member. It could not apply to a question at large, because in that way one hon. member would always have to take as gospel anything said 'by another hon. member.

speechtext:
I understood the hon.
member to say that not over two months ago they did own mines and if any change had taken place it must have been since then. That is the statement he made. He did not say that they owned any now, but that they had owned mines in the past.
The statement I made and that I know for a fact is that they did not control these mines two months ago.

I gave to the House some of my reasons for saying that Mackenzie and Mann controlled and owned these mines in Cumberland and that they owned the Canadian Collieries, Limited, two months ago. If the hon. gentleman has any facts in his possession to show that they have cased to be owners and controllers of these mines, it is due to the House that he should submit them.
The hon. gentleman is making the statement. I ask him to give the proof.
One place where he will get the information is in the return brought down to this House.

I asked Sir William
Mackenzie myself when I approached him in connection with this matter if Mackenzie and Mann controlled these mines, and he told me distinctly they did not control; they were interested, but did not control.
Who is president of the company?
I do not know.
Why did you approach him?

To endeavour to secure
a solution, knowing he was interested as one of the shareholders in the mines. He stated to me that he did not control the mines.

I think the hon. member has probably based his statement on returns brought down from my department a few weeks ago. He referred to these returns. I do not have them under my hand, but I venture to say that he will find nothing in these returns, nothing in any letter or anything else, showing what interest Mackenzie and Mann had in the Canadian Collieries Limited.

I do not wish to say that the hon. gentleman does not desire to give the truth to the House, but I agree with him that there is no correspondence brought down which will show what particular interest they had in the mines. Certainly, they were the controlling factor and their agency at Toronto was active in attempting to secure a solution of the difficulties in these particular colleries.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That is a different matter altogether.

That is not a different matter. The correspondence does not show whether Mackenzie and Mann own ten per cent, twenty per cent, or fifty per cent of this stock, but they apparently own sufficient of the stock to take such a keen interest in it that most of the correspondence on behalf of the Canadian Collieries was handled through the Toronto office. That is evidence, I think, that they have a controlling interest in these mines. I have no evidence to offer the House that Mackenzie and Mann do not now operate these mines except the word of my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens).
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to give him some information P
When I am finished-
The hon. gentleman is making a statement that is not correct, and I am in a position to give him the correct information. If he does not want it, of course he does not want it.

Mr. Speaker, I will call to your attention the fact that an hon. gentleman (Mr. Bristol), whom we seldom see in this House except when Mackenzie, Mann and Company are under consideration, has said that I have made a statement that is not correct. I think that is not parliamentary.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The statement that what an hon. member has said is not correct is certainly parliamentary.
The hon. gentleman made a certain statement in this House. Knowing that the statement that he had made was incorrect, I said that I would give him information that was accurate.

If the hon. gentleman has any facts to give the House he will have sufficient time to give them. Only a few days ago I met a gentleman in this city who has been attempting to bring about a solution of this difficulty, and he said that he had been approached by Sir William Mackenzie more than a month ago in reference to this question. If he has no stock in the Canadian Collieries, Limited, why should he be interested in securing a settlement of this strike ?
Was that question directed at me ?

I did not ask any question at all; I asked the question generally. My hon. friend is always anxious to uphold Mackenzie and Mann. I do not blame him for it. I suppose that it is to his interests either politically or personally, I do not know which. I am trying to be fair in this matter. The Prime Minister, the other day, was kind enough to say that he would take this question into consideration, and if the Prime Minister will say to the House that, on the information he has, Mackenzie and Mann are not interested in the collieries in British Columbia in which there is a strike at this time, I will be most happy to take his word. But I cannot take the word of every hon. gentleman behind him who pops up in his place and says that he knows that they have no interest in those mines-
Nobody has said that.

-unless he is able to substantiate that statement. Objection was taken to this motion because there has been no request made by the operatives of British Columbia for ,a>
settlement of this strike. I understand that there has been. I am only speaking from what I have been told. A gentleman who has been president of the Trades and Labour Council of Canada assured me that there had been laid before the Department of Labour a basis of settlement on behalf of the striking miners. That statement was made to me only three days -ago by Mr. Watters who is, I think, now president of the Trades and Labour Council. But even if thfere was not an actual .application made for a board of conciliation that should not put this amendment ini any other light than the true one which is that we are trying to get the people together and to .arrive at an equitable land fair basis of settlement of the coal shrike in British Columbia. My hon. friend from Vancouver has said that he would venture the assertion that neither the mover of this resolution nor myself, the seconder, had ever approached the Minister of Labour towards getting .a settlement of this trouble. The hon. gentleman is right in that. I have never approached hiim but when the question was up in the House during the present session we expressed our views and sentiments and said that something should be done, and could be done, by the Minister of Labour to bring about a settlement of this strike. The Minister of Labour was

kind enough to acknowledge the tact that under an Act of Parliament, the Conciliation Act, he couild appoint a boaird to inquire into the facts and ascertain who was right and who was wrong.
I am aorry to have heard the hon. member for Vancouver say that he had sacrificed his time in attempting to get a settlement of this strike. This is the first time I have ever heard a public man in this country say that he was sacrificing his time in endeavouring to get a settlement of a strike that has been a horror in the coal mining districts of British Columbia for a couple of years. He is sent here by the people of British Columbia to do just 'such things, he is sent here by the electors of the city of Vancouver in the public interest and when he tells this House and the country that he is sacrificing his time in doling that he is certainly saying what no other public man in Canada has ever dared to say.

Mr. PORTER moved the second reading of Bill No. 220, for the relief of Helen Vine-berg.

Before this Bill is read the second time, I desire to say that my attention has been called to the circumstances of this case. The well-understood practice of this House, in dealing with Divorce Bills from the Senate, is to treat the conclusions arrived at by the Senate Committee as being proper findings of facts, unless they appear to not to be justified Iby or to be contrary to the evidence. My opinion is that any lawyer who reads the testimony-and it is not very interesting testimony to read-will agree that there is absolutely no warrant or foundation for their finding that adultery was committed in this particular case. It is true, there is evidence of other circumstances as to the relations between the parties, on whicli some comments might be made; but I do not understand that, as a matter of law, these facts or circumstances furnish any contributory reasons why a divorce should be granted. On the main question, which is the usual ground upon which a divorce should be granted, I submit that the evidence is not only not in favour of the petitioner, but distinctly to the contrary.
The circumstances are that a servant-maid in the house of the respondent and the petitioner gave certain evidence alleging the paternity of a child that was born, and stated that the respondent was the parent. This is absolutely denied by the respondent, who also denies categorically the circumstances alleged by this witness. He is supported in his denial by the fact that the woman referred to had sworn, of her own free will and accord in Toronto, that the paternity of the child belonged to another party. Any man in this country

could be attacked and placed in a very unfortunate position if evidence of this character were held to be sufficient to warrant the granting of a divorce. I have been at a loss to understand the motives which led the gentlemen who compose the Divorce Committee in the Senate to come to this conclusion. Were it a case in which the	reliability of the
parties would form an issue and in which the judges, whose duty it was to determine the facts), might have the advantage of seeing the parties in arriving at a conclusion, I would not question the decision at which they arrived; but the evidence is of such a character that the truth or falsity of the allegation cannot be determined by any such means. We have here, therefore, a case in which the other branch of this Parliament, where these Bills are initiated, has undertaken to make a finding which I am sure any lawyer in this House who reads the testimony will agree with me is contrary to the evidence. Personally I do not desire to accept the responsibility of giving the second reading to a Bill which is in that position. While I do not think as a rule this House should interfere in pure questions of fact, where the elements of forming judgment Test peculiarly with the committee of the other House, that is not the case here. No court of appeal in my judgment, after reading this testimony would come to any other conclusion than that the findings of fact were contrary to the evidence. I would therefore respectfully protest against this Bill being read the second time on that evidence.
i Mr. THOBURN:	I do not know what
decision lawyers might come to upon reading the evidence; but I feel satisfied, as one who heard the evidence, that not only lawyers but every one else who heard it would be perfectly satisfied that the applicant in this case was justified in getting her divorce. As one of the sub-committee appointed to hear these cases, I heard the evidence and I confess I do not expect ever to hear such evidence again. I do not think such evidence was ever before submitted to a court. The act of adultery is proven beyond a doubt; time and places on several occasion, day and date, were given, which I do not think could be contradicted.
It was contradicted, as a matter of fact.
By the defendant?
And by the previous sworn testimony of the girl.

You could hardly expect anything else. There are not many defendants who will, as a rule, acknowledge the charge made against them. I have every reason to believe, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill should get its second reading. It was heard before the Senate Committee on two occasions, and I might say that on neither of these occasions was there a dissenting voice. It passed the Senate by a two-thirds majority, and I hope and trust if it comes to this House it will pass likewise.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like to say with regard to this amendment, as a question of order was raised before 6 o'clock, that I have looked info it carefully. At first it seemed to me to be not in order. The amendment is based on several allegations. One is that Mackenzie and Mann own coal mines in British Columbia, an allegation of fact; another is an implied allegation, that they are the owners of coal mines at which there is a strike; and the third is an allegation of fact that the operatives in these mines had requested that a conciliation board be appointed. As these are allegations of fact, with which, of course, the Speaker could not be familiar, nor could he be expected to decide, I think that it must be left to the House to decide the question. Therefore, I rule that the amendment is in order.

Mr. Speaker, when I arose before dinner to speak on the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville), I intended to say but a very few words, and to give my reasons for supporting the amendment and for giving my name as its seconder. There were some statements challenged by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, and there seems to be some doubt as to whether or not Messrs'. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, or the Canadian Northern Railway Company, are interested in these mines in British Columbia. I propose, therefore, to read certain correspondence

which, took place between the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Department of Labour.

If the hon. gentleman refers to me, there was no assertion made that the Canadian Northern Railway Company or Mackenzie, Mann and Company were not interested in any of the mines in Vancouver island. The statement I made was that the Canadian Northern, or Mackenzie, Mann and Company, do not control one single mine on Vancouver island at the present time.

I am going to give to
this House very strong testimony from the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the officials of Mackenzie and Mann, as well as from the private secretary of Sir William Mackenzie, which will remove any doubt that the Canadian Northern or Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann did control 'and operate the mines in British Columbia when this strike became prevalent on the 4th of September, 1912.
On September 4, 1912, the following letter was addressed by Mr. D. B. Hanna, third vice-president of the Canadian Northern railway, to F. A. AoLamd, the Deputy Minister of Labour. It seems' there was some correspondence before this, but I am starting wiith this particular communication :
Toronto, Ont., Sept. 4,. 1912.
F. A. Acland, Esq.,
Deputy Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ont.
Your message 21st only received yesterday, but not on being on board I waited to consult Sir William and have since wired Victoria for information, we thank minister for his offer and will state situation more fully when 1 receive reply from Victoria. Meanwhile understand men at one mine have quit work but trouble not spreading.
(Sgd) D. B. Hanna.
On the 27th of September, 1912, Mr. Acland writes to Mr. Hanna as follows:
Ottawa, Sept. 27, 1912.
Re disturbances in coal mines at Ladysmith and Cumberland, B.C.
Dear Sir,-With further reference to the industrial troubles in the coal mines controlled by your company on Vancouver island concerning which the department has exchanged telegrams with you, the minister, I am to state, is particularly desirous of having without delay your company's statement on the subject, and would he obliged if the same could he forwarded immediately. Statements received by the minister go to show that work has ceased at Ladysmith as well as Cumberland, the alleged ground being discrimination against membership in the local union, hut the department is not fully informed as to this. The situation is one in
[Mr. Carroll. |
which it w'ould appear probable that an application would shortly be received for a board of conciliation and investigation, and the minister has thought that your company might desire to take action which will render unnecessary the establishment of such a board. Can you kindly arrange to have a statement expressing the company's view forwarded to the department so that it may be placed before the minister on Monday, the 30th.
Yours very truly,
9 p.m.	(Sgd) F. A. Acland,
Deputy Minister of Labour. D. B. Hanna, Esq.,
Third Vice-Pres., Canadian Northern Ry., Toronto, Ont.
I wish to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the House, that Mr. Acland says that ' industrial troubles ' have arisen ' in the coal mines controlled by your company ' and that this epistle is addressed to the third vice-president of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Mr. Acland [DOT]again writes Mr. Hanna on the 19th of November:
Dear Mr. Hanna:
When I called on you on the 9th instant regarding the coal mining troubles of your company's mines on Vancouver island you were good enough to promise to secure a statement of circumstances to date and asked your Mr. Thompson to see to it. I had intended calling on you on the following Saturday, the ICth inst., but did not reach Toronto until your offices were closed. Perhaps you will he kind enough to forward for the minister's information the statement you were expecting, if it has in the meantime, arrived. Parliament, as you are aware, meets immediately and the minister feels it would be well to have the latest information from the company's point of view as to this somewhat difficult dispute.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) F. A. Acland, Deputy Minister of Labour.
D. B. Hanna, Esq.,
Third Vice-Pres., Canadian Northern Railway, Toronto, Ont.
Surely nobody can dispute that between September 27, when the first letter was directed to Mr. Hamma saying that industrial troubles had occurred in the coal mines ' controlled ' by his company in Vancouver, and the letter of the 19th of November which refers to ' the coal mining troubles of your company's mines on Vancouver island,' Mackenzie, Mann and Company were interested. If they were not interested they certainly should have denied it.
On the 21st of November the answer of Mr. Hanna, follows:
F. A. Acland, Esq.,
Deputy Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Acland,-I have your letter of the 19th instant. I understand from Mr. F. C. Annesley, secretary to our president, that he

sent to Sir William at Ottawa on the 18th instant some papers concerning the difficulty at the mines on Vancouver island, and no doubt Sir William has since taken the matter up with you.
Will you please advise me if such is not the
case?
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) D. B. Hanna.
It- is not difficult, of course, to identify the Sir William referred to in this letter; he is none other than Sir William Mackenzie, president of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Mr. Acland answers this letter on November 23, 1912, as follows:
Dear Mr. Hanna,-Yours of the 21st. Sir William, as you say, has been in Ottawa for some days, but has not, I think, been in the department and has not left with the minister or elsewhere any papers or information concerning the difficulties at your mines. If you are able to apprise the minister of the latest developments and present situation it would be an advantage. It frequently happens that questions on matters of this kind are asked in Parliament and the minister particularly desires to have information at hand.
Yours truly,
P. A. Acland,
Deputy Minister of Labour.
D. B. Hanna, Esq.,
Third Vice-President,
Canadian Northern Railway Company, Toronto, Ont.
Then comes a letter from a gentleman who, I understand, is Sir William Mackenzie's private secretary. It is as follows:
Hon. P. A. Acland,
Deputy Minister of Labour,
*	Ottawa Ont.
Dear Sir,-With regard to your letter to Mr. D. B. Hanna, respecting trouble at the local mines, Sir William Mackenzie is going to Ottawa to-night. Will you therefore kindly communicate with him while there. I may say that we understood that Colonel Davidson had seen either you or the minister with regard to this matter.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) H. Annesley.
I am not in a position to say who Colonel Davidson is, but I understand from an lion, gentleman in front of me that he is the land agent of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. But the most wonderful telegram of all is one which was sent from Cumberland by one of the mine managers, a man by the name of Coulson. It is a private telegram, but it was brought down in the files produced by the Labour Department at the request of the hon. member for Maisonneuve. It is between officials of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and not between the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Department of Labour, and I am at
a loss to understand how it came to be brought down. It was sent by one of the coal mine managers at Cumberland to Sir William Mackenzie and was forwarded to him by Mr. Annesley, Mr. Mackenzie's private secretary. It is as follows:
Canadian Northern Railway Company, Offices of the Third Vice-President,
Toronto, Ont., October 7, 1912. Translation of message to Sir William Mackenzie :
Coulson Wires:
Replying to my telegram of the 10th, I did not state that two weeks ago our miners were prevented from voting on resumption work by local union president, who destroyed ballot boxes and also threatened men. Local union officials realize error in not giving thirty days' notice before striking and also in not having consulted international union and are trying to avert responsibility. International union repudiate action and will not support strike morally or financially. Conditions very quiet but we expect men very soon to hold indignation meeting and return to work repudiating union entirely.
Here comes a very important part of the telegram:
Union appeals to Ottawa their last resort. If unsuccessful union dead and labour trouble ended.
If there were any doubt as to what conclusion should be arrived at from the letters which I have read concerning the control of those mines by the Canadian Northern Railway Company, there can be no doubt about it after reading this message from the manager of those mines, directed to Sir William Mackenzie, in which he denies that the company's miners were prevented from voting at a certain election held among the miners. I am sorry that I had to read all those letters, but I place them on record to show that in my humble judgment when this strike was in progress in 1912 and 1913, Mackenzie and Mann, or the Candian Northern Railway Company, controlled and were developing certain mines in the province of British Columbia. If since that time the control has been handed over to other parties, and I do not say that it has not, there may be some reason for hon. gentlemen opposite saying that this amendment is out of order and should not be voted upon. Nothing, has been done, however; and the strike is still on. I hold in my hand a paper called the Industrial Banner, dated May 22, 1914, in which there is a .telegram from British Columbia to the eeffot that the strike is still on though it is not so serious. There has been so much discussion as to who is in the wrong in this matter that I think now is the time and place to have it

shown exactly why matters came to the crisis that they reached in the coal mining areas of British Columbia. If Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann or the Canadian Northern Bailway Company have nothing to do with those mines, this amendment is not going to hurt them; they can easily prove to the gentlemen who have special control of this legislation that they are not interested in the mines. I hope, however, that if they are called upon they will give their own evidence, and not ask the clerks in their office to produce the necessary proof. The question was threshed out in the House as to whether or not the Labour Department, presided over by the hon. the Minister of Labour, whom I am glad to see in the House again after his illness, was to blame in this matter. We criticised the department in the House some time ago and we tried to cast upon them the onus of showing wffiat they had done in connection with the matter; we believed that they had done nothing. I am not going to reiterate those statements, but as a matter of fact nothing has been done, whether it is the fault of the Labour Department, the Canadian Collieries, Limited or the Canadian Northern Bailway Company I am not going to say. But it is certainly due to labour and capitalistic interests in this country that this matter should be settled peaceably and amicably. The hon. member for Vancouver said that last year he sacrificed his time and energy towards the settlement of this strike; sacrificed, mark you, Mr. Speaker, his time and energy.

I think that the hon.
member is getting outside of the amendment. The matter for discussion now' is not the strike, 'but the question of the amendment to the third reading of this Bill.

I was -attempting to show why the Government should accept this amendment, and I was giving the reasons wffiich prompted me to accept it. Of course, if I am not allowed to give my reasons for supporting the amendment I presume that I am out of order. The hon. member for Vancouver said that he sacrificed much time and energy in promoting the interests of the miners of British Columbia. I am sorry that any hon. gentleman in this House should think that the devotion of time and energy to such a purpose is a sacrifice. If he has given time and energy to the solution of this difficult problem, it has met with very little success; it has borne very little fruit, 
because the trouble still exists, though it is not so acute as it was three or four months ago. I can do nothing else than give this amendment my cordial support; I think it deserves the support of every well-thinking and reasonable man in this House. The Government had due notice when this Bill was in committee that such an amendment would be offered. If they have any very good reason for not giving it consideration and not adopting the amendment, we on this side will be well satisfied; but we wTould like to hear some other reasons udiy the Government at this particular stage should not accept this amendment when they have played the same role heretofore, or told the country that they have played that role heretofore in settling a difficult problem in connection with the Grand Trunk Bailway system. So they cannot say that they have no precedent, that they have not set a precedent for settling labour troubles along the line here suggested.
