Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 185, for the relief of the depositors of The Farmers Bank of Canada. He said:
Mr. Speaker, before entering upon my

argument in support of this measure, I propose to give a brief history of the bank to which it relates and the various steps and proceedings which have led up to this resolution. The Farmers Bunk of Canada was incorporated in the year 1904, the incorporators being: James Gallagher, Teeswater; John Watson, Listowel; John Ferguson and Alexander Fraser, Toronto; and Alexander S. Lowe, Drayton. These gentlemen were named in the Act as provisional directors. During the sessions of 1905 and 1906 extensions of time were granted within which the bank might obtain the certificate of the Treasury Board which was necessary under the provisions of the Bank Act, for the commencement of its business. Finally, on November 30, 1906, the Treasury Board issued its certificate and the bank entered upon its career. The head office of the bank was established at the city of Toronto and its branches were principally in the rural districts of Ontario. The name of the bank was evidently designed by the promoters to attract farmers as depositors and customers, and they succeeded in their purpose, because the principal part of their deposits and business was drawn from that source. After carrying on the business of banking for four years the bank suspended payment on December 19, 1910, and has, since that date, been in process of liquidation.
The failure of the bank caused a sensation at the time on account of its unprecedentedly disastrous character and on account of the reports that speedily obtained currency as to the nature of the transactions in which the money of the bank had been lost. Allegations were made at the time that the issue of the certificate of the Treasury Board in the year 1906 had been procured by fraud and deceit on the part of Travers, the general manager of the bank, whose dishonesty had been the cause of the wreck. It was further alleged that the Government of the day had had express notice of such fraud and deceit and should not have issued the certificate. On this ground it was then urged that the Government was responsible for the loss which had ensued both to depositors and shareholders. During the session of 1910-11 a petition was presented to my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) then the leader of the Government, and his Finance Minister, the Hon. Mr. Fielding, for parliamentary relief to both depositors and shareholders upon the following grounds:
(1)	That a certificate to open the hank should not have been granted;

(2)	That the certificate which was issued should have been subsequently cancelled;
(3)	That the shareholders should be released from the claim for double liability; and
(4)	That the depositors should be compensated for the loss of their deposits.
The subject of this petition was discussed in the House during the session of 1910-11 upon a motion made by my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson), which motion was as follows:
That this House is of opinion that a Royal Commission should forthwith issue to inquire into and investigate the incorporation and organization of the Farmers' Bank of Canada and the granting of a certificate by the Treasury Board permitting such bank to issue notes and transact business and al the circumstances connected therewith, and generally to inquire into and investigate the operation and efficiency of the Bank Act in relation to the affairs and transactions of the said bank.
In the debate upon that motion, particulars were given of the alleged negligence on the part of the Treasury Board in granting the certificate. At this point it will be informing to the House to call attention to certain provisions: existing in the then Bank Act, and I desire to place them upon ' Hansard ' because they have a bearing upon the question of the alleged negligence of the Treasury Board, and upon the arguments which I shall adduce in respect thereto.
Clause 12: For the purpose of organizing the bank the provisional directors may after giving public notice thereof cause stock books to be opened in which shall be recorded the subscriptions of such prsons as desire to become shareholders in the bank.
Clause 13: So soon as a sum not less than $500,000 of the capital stock of the bank has been bona fide subscribed and a sum not less tlfan $250,000 thereof has been paid to the minister, the provisional directors may by public notice, published for at least four weeks, call a meeting of the subscribers to the said stock, to be held, etc., and the subscribers at such meeting shall (a) determine the day upon which the annual general meeting of the bank is to be held; and (b) elect such number of directors duly qualified under this Act, not less than five, as they may think necessary.
Clause 14 : The bank shall not issue notes or commence the business of banking until it has obtained from the Treasury Board a certflcate permitting it to do so.
Clause 15 : No certificate shall be given by the Treasury Board until it has been shown to the satisfaction of the board by affidavit or otherwise that all the requirements of this Act, and of the said Aot of incorporation of the bank as to the payment required to be made to the minister, the election of directors, the deposit for security for note issue, or other preliminaries, have been complied with, and that the sum so paid is then held by the minister.
These were the provisions of the Bank Act with which it was necessary that the

provisional directors of the bank should comply before they were entitled to the issue of the certificate by the Treasury Board. I would call particular attention, although I hardly think it is necessary, to this provision of clause 13:
So soon as a sum of not less than $500,000 of the capital stock of the bank has been bona fide subscribed, and a sum not less than $250,000 thereof has been paid to the minister.
Because the argument will turn to a certain extent upon the provision of the Bank Act contained in that clause.
It was charged in the House in the course of the debate that bona fide certificates to the amount of $500,000 never were received, that bona fide payments on account thereof never were made, and that no authority ever was given by the subscribers to apply for a certificate to open the bank. It was charged further: that the certificate of the Treasury Board was obtained by fraud, deceit, and perjury of W. B. Travers the General Manager of the bank; and it was alleged that the Treasury Board, through the Minister of Finance, had express notice by a letter from Leighton McCarthy, K.C., M.P., addressed to the minister, and secondly by verbal notice from David Henderson, M.P., and Sir Edmund Osier, that fraud was being practised in the application for the certificate of the Treasury Board. I desire to place upon ' Hansard ' the letters which will be found in the Sessional Papers for the year 1911, forming the correspondence which passed between Mr. Leighton McCarthy and others, and the department. I read first a letter of October 8, 1906, addressed from Leighton McCarthy, K.C., M.P., to the Hon. Mr. Fielding, Minister of Finance at Ottawa:
Toronto, Oct. 8, 1906.
Hon. W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.	[DOT]
My dear Mr. Fielding,-I have been consulted on behalf of a number of subscribers to the shares of the Farmers' Bank, and from the instructions I have received a number of the subscribers will dispute the bona fide character of the subscriptions. I have not time to-night to give a full statement of the grounds of this request to you, but I beg to assure you that grave conditions have arisen which will require careful consideration before the Treasury Board would grant any certificate for the organization of this bank.
I therefore ask you to be good enough to stay any action 'which might be taken until I have had an opportunity of discussing this with you. If it is not asking you to hold it too long, I would prefer not having to go to Ottawa this week, but will go any day next week which would suit your convenience. Of course if 295
there is no immediate prospect of your granting such a certificate my seeing you at an early date will not be necessary.
Leighton McCarthy.
On October 11 another communication was addressed to the Minister of Finance by Mr. Leighton McCarthy, as follows:
Toronto, Oct. 11, 1906.
Hon. W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Please wire me assurance in reference to stay of certificate of Treasury Board mentioned in my letter of Monday night.
Leighton McCarthy.
Again, on October 11, 1906, Mr. Fielding addressed a telegram to Mr. McCarthy, evidently in answer to the one I have just read:
Ottawa, October 11, 1906. Leighton McCarthy, M.P.,
Toronto.
No application yet received for the certificate referred to. Please forward your representations immediately and they will be considered when application comes.
W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance.
On October 11, Mr. Fielding wrote this letter to Mr. Leighton McCarthy:
Minister of Finance, Canada.
Ottawa, October 11, 1906. Leighton G. McCarthy, Esq., M.P.,
Toronto.
My dear Mr. McCarthy,-I have your letter of the 8th instant, and your telegram to-day on the subject of the Farmers' Bank.
I wired you to-day that no application had been made by the promoters for the Treasury Board certificate, and suggested that you send forward at once any representations which you may wish to make, to which we shall give all due consideration.
W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance.
On October 12, we have the reply from Mr. Leighton MaCarthy to the telegram of the 11th of October:
Toronto, October 12, 1906. Hon. W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
My dear Mr. Fielding,-Many thanks tor your telegram received last night, advising me that no application had yet been received for certificate of the Farmers Bank and asking me to forward representations immediately when they will be considered. This will receive my attention.
I am obliged to you for the telegram.
Leighton McCarthy.
On October 19, and this is a very important communication, Mr. McCarthy addressed the following letter to the Minister of Finance:

Toronto, Oct. 19, 1906.
Hon. W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Re the Farmers Bank of Canada.
My dear Mr. Fielding.-I beg to inclose the special endorsement upon a writ of summons in the High Court of Justice for Ontario, which will be issued by William A. Saxon, John Sproat, George Castle, William McLean, Finlay Mc-Callum, Robert Hume, James Murray, George Denoon, John McLeod, Jane Shuert, William Harris, on behalf of themselves and all other persons alleged to be subscribers for shares of the capital stock of the Farmers Bank of Canada who may desire to come in and be parties to this action, against the Farmers Bank of Canada, James Gallagher, John Watson, John Ferguson, Alexander Fraser, Alexander Shepherd, Lown, W. R. Travers, C. H. Smith, A. G. H. Luxton, and the Traders' Bank of Canada, and W. J. Lindsay and I respectfully request that the Treasury Board will stay any action upon the application of persons professing to act in the name of the Farmers Bank of Canada, or in the name of the provisional directors of the Farmers Bank of Canada, for a certificate under section 15 of the Bank Act on the grounds alleged in the inclosed special endorsement, and other grounds which may be disclosed upon the examination of the alleged subscribers for shares.
I have received information that the alleged subscribers for shares paid a large sum of money in cash and have signed notes for other large sums of money, and that the persons professing to act in the name of the bank have transferred notes and received the proceeds, and that a deposit either has been made or will be made of the cash received and the proceeds of these notes, or sufficient amount to .make up $250,000.
I wish you to have the kindness to acknowledge the receipt of this protest against the granting of a certificate so that I may advise the shareholders who are disputing their liability, and I would be pleased to go to Ottawa upon any appointment you may make for the further consideration of this matter.
Leighton McCarthy.
On October 23,	1906, that letter is
acknowledged by Mr. Boville, acting Deputy Minister of Finance, in the following communication:
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 19th inst. to Mr. Fielding's address respecting the Farmers Bank of Canada. When application is made by the Farmers Bank to the Treasury Board for a certificate to enable them to commence business, the representations contained in your letter with its enclosure will be laid before the board.
(Sgd) T. C. Boville.
For Deputy Minister of Finance.
On October 23, 1906, we have a communication from Travers addressed to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General, as follows:
Dear Sir,-I hereby beg to enclose you certificate No. 1150 from the Bank of Montreal,

Toronto, for $250,000, to be deposited to the credit of the Farmers Bank of Canada in compliance with section 13 of the Bank Act.
Please acknowledge receipt and oblige.
(Sdg) W. R. Travers,
General manager.
On October 24, 1906, we have the acknowledgement of Mr. Boville in the following terms:
The General Manager,
The Farmers Bank of Canada,
Toronto.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 23rd instant, enclosing receipt and draft of the Bank of Montreal, Toronto, for the sum of $250,000 deposited by your bank in compliance with section 13 of the Bank Act.
I may say in this connection that opposition has been filed in this department to the granting of a certificate to your bank under section 14 of the Bank Act.
T. ,C. Boville,
For Deputy Minister of Finance.
Then Mr. Travers replies on the 29th: [DOT]
Toronto, October 29, 1906. The Hon. Deputy Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir,-Yours __of the 24th, post-marked October 26, was received here on the 27th.
I was surprised to know that any one had filed an opposition against this bank being granted a certificate.
Would you kindly do me the favour of supplying me with a copy of the said objections, as I do not know up to the present moment wherein we have deviated in the slightest effect from the Bank Act.
W. R. Travers, General Manager.
Then there is a letter from Mr. Boville to Mr. Leighton McCarthy under date of October 31, 1906, as follows:
Dear Sir,-Referring to your letter of the 19 th instant, addressed to Mr. Fielding, on the subject of the Farmers Bank of Canada and the issue of a certificate to that bank to commence business under section 15 of the Bank Act, I noticed recently a reference in the newspapers for a judgment given by Judge Anglin in a suit relating to this matter. In view of the decision rendered, I shall be obliged if you will let me know if you still desire the protest contained in your letter to be brought before the Treasury Board upon an application of the Farmers Bank for a certificate to be considered.
T. C. Boville,
For Deputy Minister of Finance.
Mr. McCarthy replies, under date of November 1, 1906, as follows:
T. C. Boville, Esq.,
Acting Deputy Minister of Finance, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-With reference to yours of the 31st ultimo, I will be in Ottawa on Monday or Tuesday of next w^eek when I will do myself the pleasure of calling upon you with reference to the subject matter of your letter.
Leighton McCarthy.

Then Mr. Boville addresses a letter to Mr. Travers under date of November 2, 1906, as follows:
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt ot your letter ot the 29th instant, and in reply I beg to enclose herewith a copy of a letter addressed to Mr. Fielding by Mr. Leighton McCarthy by way of protest to the granting of a certificate to your bank to commence business. Of the enclosure with Mr. McCarthy's letter I have not sent you a copy as it is lengthy, and I have no doubt you already have a copy of it in your possession.
(Sgd) T. C. Boville,
For Deputy Minister of Finance.
Then there is a letter from Mr. Leighton McCarthy under date of November 2, 1906, addressed to Mr. Fielding, Minister of Finance, as follows:
Dear Sir,-Referring to my letters of the Sth and 9th instant, with reference to the application for a certificate made on behalf of the Farmers Bank; I am advised by those who are instructing me that the claims made by them in the action brought have been settled by their subscriptions being taken up by some parties interested in the bank and refunding the money paid by the individuals or returning the notes which had been given. The objections which I made on their behalf to the issue of the certificate are therefore withdrawn. Would you mind therefore returning to me the papers which I forwarded to you.
(Sgd) Leighton McCarthy.
Mr. Boville replies on November 7 to Mr. McCarthy:
Dear Sir,-Referring to your letter of the 2nd instant, in the matter of an application of the Farmers Bank of Canada for a certificate to commence business, I beg to enclose herewith the papers forwarded with your letter of the 19th October.
(Sgd) T. C. Boville, Deputy Minister of Finance.
The next is a letter from Mr. Boville to Mr. Travers under date of November 7, 1906:
Dear Sir,-Referring to my letter to you of the 2nd inst., inclosing copy of a letter addressed to Mr. Fielding by Mr. Leighton McCarthy by -way of a protest to the granting of a certificate to your bank to commence business, I beg to state that I am advised by Mr. McCarthy that the objections which he made to the issue of a certificate have been withdrawn.
Then there is a further letter on November 21,	1906, from Mr. Boville to Mr. Travers:
Dear Sir,-Referring to your letter of the 23rd October, making a deposit under section 13 of the Bank Act of the sum of $250,000. I have no doubt that you will be applying very shortly for a certificate under section 14 to commence business. In the papers to be submitted to the board in support of the application there is a list of bona fide subscribers of capital stock of the bank showing subscriptions to the extent of $500,000. Would you 295 i
be so good as to have added to this list for submission to the board, a statement showing the actual amount of cash paid up by each subscriber.
(Sgd) T. C. Boville, Deputy Minister of Finance.
Then there is a letter in reply to that addressed to the Deputy Minister of Finance by Travers:
Dear Sir,-I have the honour herewith to forward declaration of the general manager of the Farmers Bank of Canada setting forth facts relating to the incorporation and organization of the said bank, and also giving the names of the directors elected at the meeting of subscribers and such other particulars as are required by the Bank Act. The provisions of the Act as to subscriptions and deposit with the Receiver General having been fully complied with on behalf of the said bank, I apply for the certificate of the Treasury Board permitting the said bank to commence the business of banking.
(Sgd) W. R. Travers,
General Manager.
I will ask the House to bear in mind that the certificate of the Treasury Board was issued on the 30th day of November, 1906.
What was the date oi the last letter?

November 27, 1906. On
November 30, 1906, the following letter was addressed by Mr. Fielding, Minister of Finance, to Mr. W. R. Travers, General Manager of the Farmers5 Bank of Canada:
Dear Sir,-I regret that owing to pressing engagements yesterday, arising out of the Budget, I was unable to meet you to consider your application for the issue of a certificate to authorize the Farmers Bank of Canada to commence business. I shall be glad to see you to-day, at my office, at any time before one o'clock if you can call. Or I might be able to see you later, between four and five, at the House of Commons, if that will be more convenient.
There is a phase of the matter which I should like to bring to your notice so that you may consider it at once. It has been represented to us that in some previous instances where an application was in all respects apparently regular, there was actually an evasion of the intention of the Bank Act in relation to the paid-up capital. We have been told that in some cases the subscribers did not actually pay in cash but gave notes to the provisional directors which were used to raise the money. On account of information of this kind, which has reached us in relation to a previous case, we deem it proper to scan very closely every application for a certificate which comes to us. I shall be glad to have an assurance, that nothing of the kind has taken place in relation to the subscriptions for the Farmers Bank, but that the amounts set forth in the application as having been paid up have in every case been bona fide cash payments.
W. S. Fielding.
Minister of Finance^

On the same date is a letter from Travers in reply addressed to the hon. Minister of Finance:
Dear Sir,-In reply to your letter of the 30th of November, I have to say that in the ease of the Farmers Bank of Canada, the provisional directors did not raise the money in the way mentioned by you. You will find the statement put in by me absolutely correct as to the amount of stock subscribed and the amount paid up.
W. R. Travers,
General Manager, Farmers Bank of Canada
Both of these letters are dated November 30, 1906, and on the same date at a meeting of the Treasury Board the following minute was made:
The board had under consideration an application made by the Farmers Bank of Canada under the provisions of the Bank Act for the issue by the Treasury Board of a certificate permitting the said bank to issue notes and commence the business of banking.
It having been shown to the satisfaction of the board that all the requirements of section 15 of the said Act have been complied with the board authorize the issue of the certificate applied for.
T. C. Boville,
Secretary.
Then the certificate is in the following form; issued the same date, November 30, 1906:
This is to certify that the Treasury Board, at a meeting held on the thirtieth day of November, A.D., 1906, authorize the issue of a certificate under the provisions of the Bank Act permitting the Farmers Bank of Canada to issue notes and commence the business of banking and this certificate is hereby issued in accordance with such authority and for the purposes above mentioned.
Dated at Ottawa this thirtieth day of November, A.D., 1906.
Now, I should call attention here-I had inadvertently overlooked it-to a letter addressed by the Deputy Minister of Justice to the Deputy Minister of Finance, dated the 28th of November, 1906:
I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 28th instant, and of the inclosed papers, being the application from the Farmers Bank of Canada for a certificate to commence business, under section 13-17 of the Bank Act, and papers in support thereof.
You ask me to advise you if on the papers submitted such certificate may legally issue.
In reply, I beg to state that the statements in the statutory declaration of Mr. Walter R. Travers are sufficient, if they are accepted, to show compliance with the statutory provisions and that the evidence thus afforded is such as the Treasury Board may lawfully accept under the Act, and thereupon issue to the bank a certificate under section 14 of the Act.
Papers returned herewith.
E. L. Newcombe,
Deputy Minister of Justice.

Now, under date of November 30, 1906, there is another letter which I desire to place upon ' Hansard although it would not in the ordinary course come to hand until the day after the issue of the certificate by the Treasury Board. That letter which is referred to in the'debates on the motion to which I have alluded, and afterwards in the report of the commissioner with which I shall deal later, is addressed by Mr. E. S. Clouston, then president of the Canadian Bankers Association, to the Deputy Minister of Finance. It is as follows:
T. C. Boville, Esq.,
Deputy Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Farmers Bank of Canada.
Dear Sir,
In . connection with the application of the Farmers Bank of Canada for the usual certificate from the Treasury Board, I have reason to believe that the money lodged, or to be lodged, at Ottawa as stock subscriptions, cannot be regarded as paid-up capital, and that a large proportion of the amount necessary to the obtaining of a certificate is a loan made upon the promise of its payment when returned by your department.
Permit me to request that, if only for the protection of the public, the Treasury Board will exercise its right to refuse to issue a certificate if it thinks best so to do, until a thorough investigation has been made into the circumstances stated herein.
E. S. Clouston,
President.
To which the following reply was 'sent- and this reply, I think, ends my reading of the correspondence:
Finance Department, Ottawa, Canada, December 3, 1906
E. S. Clouston, Esq.,
President Canadian Bankers Association, Montreal, P.Q.
Dear Mr. Clouston,-I beg. to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 30th ultimo, respecting the Farmers Bank of Canada. I note what you state with regard to the money paid in under section 13 of the Bank Act.
In view of the published reports in the newspapers, of some litigation in connection with the subscriptions to the capital of this bank, the matter has had the careful attention of the department, and some time ago the general manager of the bank was communicated with to the effect that when applying for the certificate to commence business, in addition to the list of subscriptions to the extent of a half million required by the Bank Act, the statement should contain also the actual amount of cash paid up by each subscriber on his subscription. On the 29th ultimo application, in due form, was made by the bank for the certificate permitting it to commence the business of banking. The application was accompanied by the usual documents and also by a list of the subscriptions of cash paid in by each subscriber. The list itself covers over 500 names and nothing therein appeared calling

for any particular comment. From the statutory declaration of the general manager I quote the following paragraphs:-
4.	On the twenty-third day of October, 1906, there had been actually bona fide subscribed five thousand seven hundred and fifty-seven shares of the capital stock of the Farmers Bank of Canada, and I have had personal knowledge of the applications and subscriptions, and each and all of the said subscriptions is and are on the printed form of application-a copy of which is now produced and marked exhibit 'C,' to this my declaration, and that the said subscription appeared on the stock books of the said bank, and that a sum beyond $250,000 thereof in cash has been actually paid in by the subscribers of the same.
5.	Now shown to me and marked exhibit *D' to this my declaration is a list of the subscribers of the capital stock of the said bank correctly setting forth as to each subscription the name of the subscriber, his address, the number of shares subscribed for by him, the amount of such shares and the amount paid in thereon. Each of the said subscriptions is a bona fide subscription to the capital stock of the said bank.
I previously had some conversation with Mr. Fielding, who was very busy in connection with the preparation of the Budget speech, with regard to which application. But on Friday last the day after the delivery of the Budget speech Mr. Travers, the general manager, had an interview with him. In the course of this interview that gentleman gave a most positive assurance that 'not a dollar' of the amount deposited had been borrowed. For the purpose of record Mr. Fielding wrote to Mr. Travers a letter, of which I enclose a copy, asking for the assurance that the amounts set forth in the application as having been paid in were in every case bona fide cash payments. I enclose a copy of Mr. Travers' reply.
Under these circumstances there did not seem to be any warrant for the withholding of a certificate under section 14 of the Act, and, accordingly, a certificate was issued on the 30tli ultimo.
T. C. Boville,
Deputy Minister of Finance.
So much for the alleged notice to the Minister of Finance by the communications from Mr. Leighton McCarthy, prior to the issue of the certificate,'and from the president of the Canadian Bankers Association, by a communication which apparently reached the department the day after the certificate had been issued. In addition, as I said before, it was alleged that verbal notice had been given to the minister of grave irregularities in connection with the application for the Treasury Board certificate, and I desire in this connection to read from ' Hansard ' of March, 1911, the statements made by the hon. member for Halton (Mr.' Henderson) and by Sir Edmund Osier, and the replies thereto of the Hon. Mr. Fielding, the Finance Minister. I shall not, of course, read their speeches in full, but only such
portions as appear relevant and necessary in connection with my argument.
Did not these gentlemen give evidence before Sir William Meredith? Possibly this House .would rather have the evidence they gave under oath.

speechtext:
I think I am within the
rules in reading from ' Hansard ' of a previous debate relating to the matter, and there is this further consideration-because I have no desire whatever to exclude the evidence, which, as my hon. friend says, would be the best testimony-that the reading of the evidence would be a rather lengthy and tedious performance, and I think that the matter can be put very much more succinctly and 'clearly by reading extracts from ' Hansard '.
It would not be as accurate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would not be as accurate. I think I may say that the evidence given under oath is substantially the same as the .statements made in the (House during the course of that debate.
The evidence of the hon. member for Halton was very wobbly when given before the commissioner.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It will be open to my hon. friend, if he desires, to give at length the evidence of the hon. member for Halton before the commissioner. I am satisfied, having read the evidence and having read ' Hansard,' that there is no substantial difference between the statements made in the House and those made on oath by all parties concerned. I shall read Mr. Fielding's reply to the allegations made by the hon. member for Halton and by Sir Edmund Osier. The following is an extract from the speech of the hon. member for Halt-on:
I told him-
That is, the Minister of Finance.

I was deeply interested in the matter of the Farmers Bank for the reason that a very large amount of money, practically half the stock of the hank, was subscribed in my county. I realized at this time that it might create a panic In the county if the worst came to the worst, and the bank should fail and the double liability be exacted. I told him that I myself had seen promissory notes made by farmers in my county, indorsed by the provisional directors, that had been used, as I was informed and verily believed, for the purpose of raising money presumably to make up the $250,000 required in order to get a certificate.

I have always
wondered, what notes the hon. member for Halton saw; I have assumed that they were the notes which were sued upon by Mr. McCarthy and which were returned. Is that the impression of the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not in a position to say whether the hon. member for Halton referred to the particular notes in respect of which Mr. McCarthy addressed his communication to the minister, or to other notes. My hon. friend As aw.are that promissory notes, were given by subscribers ;and afterwards hypothecated and that the money was raised in that way. Whether these particular notes were those or some of those referred to by Mr. McCarthy or whether they were some not referred to by him, I am unable to say. The hon. member for Halton goes on:
No other money was wanted by the provisional directors. They did not require to borrow money for any other purpose; they had no authority to borrow money at all, and this borrowing was altogether improper. Now, I made that statement, and X thought that was a warning to the Minister of Finance to beware of the men with whom he was dealing, and that he should he on his guard. The Minister of Finance accepted my statement in that light, and, as I said, with all the courtesy that was required, he told me that he would hold the certificate back as long as he could. X confess that I left the Minister of Finance feeling quite safe. I thought the matter was in the strong hands of a strong man, who stood between the subscribers to this stock and the Government, a man who was in a position to defend my constituents and prevent them being defrauded. Shortly afterward, the minister met me in the corridor-there was no secrecy about this conversation, never so intended by me, or I believe, by the minister

and informed me that Mr. Travers had been down, and that he had brought his money. And the minister said-(I will use his own words)- ' I put it up to him and he denied it.' What was it the minister 'put up to him?' What did the minister wish me to understand he had ' put up to him,' but the very statement I had made to him a short time before? And Mr. Travers denied it. He then asked Mr. Travers to give him a letter to that effect, declaring that my statement was untrue. And he accepted that letter and gave Mr. Travers this certificate. He believed Mr. Travers whom he had never met, perhaps, until a few days before-because I believe he was introduced to him by Mr. Calvert,-he accepted Travers' words, and repudiated mine, although I had sat in the House with him for fifteen years and we had always been on the best of terms, t confess that, when I heard the minister say, in answer to a question in this House that 4 certain gossip ' had come to him, X felt somewhat hurt; and I am delighted today to hear the minister say that in using these words he had no reference to myself, and I candidly believe he had not. . . . As I say, I called on the minister and told him that, owing to the correspondence that appeared

in the paper, I thought there was danger to the Farmers Bank. The minister was familiar with what had taken place, and, seeing that I was somewhat worried over the matter, he very kindly said to me, * Henderson, I don't see why you should worry over this; you are not responsible ; besides, you did warn the Government.' Those were the explicit words of the Minister of Finance.
Mr. Fielding: I am bound to say to my it.,', friend (Mr. Henderson) that X shall have 10 take exception to that statement later on.
Mr. Henderson: I make that statement of ray own knowledge, from distinct recollection;- and you can understand, Sir, and I think the House will understand, how vividly it was impressed upon my mind from what I have said of the anxiety I had concerning the standing of this bank. The minister says he will have to take exception to my statement, but I must ask him, as one member of this House, as one has a right to ask another, to accept this statement. I will not put it in the extreme form, but I adhere to it; the statement I made is absolutely correct.-' Hansard ', vol. Ill, 1910-11, March 15 pages 5302-5304.
Mr. Fielding replied to the statement of the hon. member for Halton as follows.

I am not going
to ask my hon. friend not to proceed, but I do not want to stay that I do not think it is fair to make that statement a part of the Government's case under this Bill when the evidence of the hon. member for Halton was taken under Oiath before the commission and is available to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I explain to my hon. friend that Mr. Fielding's reply is, I think, quite as strong as his evidence in the matter. I am putting the matter this way for the sake of convenience, and because the statements both of the hon. member for Halton and of the then Minister of Finance are in much more succinct farm heie than they are in the evidence. Mr. Fielding's reply, in so far as it related to the allegations in question, was as follows:
Now, we come to the second question, the granting of the certificate. I want to say in that connection that my chief regret is that I have to have a difference of opinion with my respected friend from Halton. I know him too well to hesitate for a moment in accepting any statement that he might make. I credit him with all good faith and sincerity, and if he and I do not agree as to what has occurred that does not imply that I for one moment question the good faith or veracity of my hon. friend, but it simply means that I am obliged to sav that my hon. friend is mistaken. I am obliged to say when my hon. friend tells me that he warned me against the issue of that certificate that he is mistaken. My hon. friend and I have had frequent conversations over the question of this bank. I do not recall, however, that we met in any formal way, but we met at different times as members of the House do,

46S3
and we had conversations concerning the bank. That arose from the fact that my hon. friend knew I was opposed to the granting of the charter and that I viewed it with anxiety. The conversations between my hon. friend and myself were always along the line that we regretted the necessity for the creation of this Farmers . Bank, we were sorry to have the farmers of the country engaging in banking when, in the case of many of them, they were not familiar with the responsibilities which would be involved in the acceptance of shares of a bank. All our conversations were along that line. We were feeling sorry that the farmers were going into this matter, hut I can assure my hon. friend that when he soys that he warned me against the issue of the certificate, although I know he makes the statement in all good faith, I am bound to say that to the best of my recollection he is entirely mistaken. Nothing of the kind occurred.
Would the minister mind reading, from the bottom of th-e page, Mr. Fielding's answer to Mr. Foster?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Foster: Does my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) wish that denial to apply to the three interviews at which there were conversations or only to the last one?
Mr. Fielding: I do not remember how many conversations I had with my hon. friend.
Mr. Foster: There were three that were mentioned.
Mr. Fielding: No matter how many there were, in so far as they took place before the issue of the certificate, I mean my denial to apply to all.
Did the hon. member for Halton, in the statement from which the minister has just read, protest against the issue of the certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He says:
Now, I made that statement, and I thought that was a warning to the Minister of Finance to beware of the men with whom he was dealing, and that he should be on his guard. The Minister of Finance accepted my statement in that light, and, as I said, with all the courtesy that was required, he told me that he would hold the certificate back as long as he could. I confess that I left the Minister of Finance feeling quite safe.
That is the discussion that took place in the House between the hon. member for Halton and the Finance Minister relating to the alleged verbal notice.
On July 28, 1911, Sir Edmund Osier spoke as follows in the House:
My attention was called, since I returned, to a debate in Parliament on the 15th of March. Before I left this country on January I was present -when we were discussing the question of the Farmers' Bank.
I then made the statement that I had spoken to the Minister of Finance in reference to the issue of a certificate to this bank. The Minister of Finance said that if I was in the House
he w-as sure I would not make that statement. After the deposit had been made with the Receiver General and before the certificate had been issued, I met the Minister of Finance and had a talk with him about the Farmers' Bank.
X told him that it was a fraud, that the people connected with it were not worthy, and that the method taken for obtaining the necessary deposit was absolutely illegal. I knew that of my own personal knowledge, because I knew where application had been made to borrow the money on these endorsed notes; I did not know at the time from whom. I saw that the Finance Minister was under a good deal of anxiety about the condition of affairs. The matter ended there so far as I was concerned until some time afterwards, when I learned that a certificate had been issued, and I again spoke to the Minister, and said I was exceedingly sorry that the Government had issued the certificate. The Finance Minister said that so far as he saw, the law had been complied with, and that if the Government had not issued the certificate they would have been open to the charge of protecting the larger banks. Of course there is a good deal of reason in that, but I think it was a case where the closest scrutiny ought to have been observed. It was notorious that the men at the head of the bank were not worthy. The information I think was given fairly, and without any prejudice against the establishment of new banks. Further than that, I may say that X had a conversation with my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson), and he told me that he had made the same representation to the Finance Minister-I only make this statement because I do not want to put in the mouth of the leader of the Opposition statements which I cannot confirm.
Mr. Fielding replied to that statement of Sir Edmund Osier as follows:
If I had been aware that the hon. gentleman intended to bring this matter up to-day I should have read over the debate to see how far there was any conflict between the hon. gentleman's statement and my own. I am quite sure any statement the hon. gentleman makes, either at this time or any other time, has been made in good faith. Busy men hesitate to speak with confidence concerning conversations that took place several years ago, and I feel that I should hesitate to speak definitely about a conversation on that matter of several years ago. But this I do know, that the attitude of my mind with relation to the Farmers' Bank was such that if my hon. friend or anybody else had given me any substantial reason against the issue of that certificate, I would have welcomed it, because it is notorious that I did not wish to issue the certificate to the Farmer's Bank. My hon. friend is right, X viewed it from the beginning with anxiety. I do remember I had a conversation with him about the matter, but I do not remember that he gave me any information bearing on the subject which would justify me in refusing to issue the certificate. I am sure, in a matter of such importance, my hon. friend if he had felt that he had material evidence to submit, would not have been content to trust the matter to memory, but he would have sent me a communication giving me definite information. It is, however, beyond question that anything that came to me on the subject from any quarter represented the anxiety which business- men had concerning the flotation of

this bankj, an anxiety which I felt. But against that, I had the sworn testimony of the man who came into my office and swore that he had complied with all the provisions of the law. That sworn testimony should have outweighed probably any casual conversation I may have had from any quarter at all. I do not for a moment imagine that the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) did anything in this matter except with the best intentions, and I am quite sure that neither he nor I have any desire to misrepresent one another.
That covers the statement made by the hon. member for Halton and the hon. member for West Toronto with respect to the alleged verbal notice given to the Minister of Finance. In order that the House may have before it the view that prevailed at the time in the House of Commons on the part of some of those now connected with the Government, I desire to refer briefly to the speech of the Eight Hon. Mr. Borden, now Prime Minister. I think it is important that the view which he took of the matter at that time should be now placed before the House.
Mr. A. K. MiACLEAN: In 1911 the Prime Minister said that if he was returned to power he would appoint a commission to look into the matter. I presume he meant that if the commission reported that there *was a just claim on behalf of depositors he would pay it; if not, he would not. It was just prior to an election, it will be remembered, that the statements which the minister is about to read were made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Borden, speaking on the motion of the hon. member for Halton, and referring to a letter which he had received, made the following statement:
That gives an idea of the way this matter Is regarded throughout the country, of the suffering which has been brought upon the people, and the question is: How has all this result been brought about? The bank obviously should not have been permitted to commence business. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance himself has admitted that. There can be no doubt at all, as my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has pointed out, that if he had taken the ordinary business precaution of calling for the minute books of this bank, as one would suppose that any man in his senses would have done, he would have seen that the Bank Act was being violated, he would not have permitted the bank to commence business.
Then he goes on to refer to the communication I have read in regard to it. He make3 the following observations:
There was the letter of Mr. Leighton McCarthy, there was the writ, and the endorsement upon the writ itself which, in the plainest and most unmistakable terms, conveyed a warning to the Minister of Finance in this

regard. Perhaps sufficient emphasis has not been laid upon one particular paragraph of Mr. McCarthy's letter of the 19th of October, 1906, three days before the writ was issued. He stated the writ would shortly be issued, and three days afterwards on the 22nd of October, it was issued, and in his letter he says:	.
I have received information that the alleged subscribers for shares paid a large sum of money in cash and have signed notes for other large sums of money, and that the persons professing to act in the name of the hank have transferred notes and received the proceeds, and that a deposit either has been made or will he made of the cash received and the proceeds of these notes, or sufficient amount to make up $250,000.	.
The intimation conveyed by that to any one who is familiar with the provisions of the Bank Act is simply that these men were conspiring together to contravene and to evade the provisions of the Act which the Minister of Finance was bound to see observed. From first to last Mr. Leighton McCarthy, in the correspondence at least, has never withdrawn the statement made by him in that letter of the 19th October, 1906. True, he did in a subsequent letter state that his clients had been settled with, hut he never in any letter withdrew these statements of fact which he made to the Minister of Finance. The statements in the writ itself are so startling and convey so plain a notice to the Minister of Finance that one would think there could not be the slightest doubt in his mind as to what his plain duty would be. The first charge of fraud is this:
1. That the provisional directors who professed to act for and in the name of the bank had no lawful power or authority to receive subscriptions for shares or to accept them; and (2) that the subscriptions for shares which were procured from the plaintiffs and others were procured through fraud and misrepresentation, and the plaintiffs allege, amongst others, the following particulars of fraud, namely:
1. That the agent in procuring the subscriptions for shares falsely represented that persons had subscribed for a larger number of shares than they had in fact subscribed for, and the following are examples of such false representations.
Did the commissioner make any finding for or against anything of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will deal with that later on. I said that before entering into a discussion of the report of the commission, which is the foundation of the legislation we are introducing, I proposed to review the steps leading up to this legislation. If I am out of order I shall how to the ruling of the Chair.
Mr. SPlEAKEK: The hon. minister is quite in order; it is not a discussion of the present session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not my desire to deal unfairly with this matter. When an allegation is made, and a reply to it is made by the minister or any one else, I

shall be glad to give it with sufficient fulness to show the attitude of the party against whom the accusation is made, and I think I have done that fairly.
The hon. unember for Halton made the statement in this House that he had given notice of irregularities to the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance denied that he had. Sir Edmund Osier made a similar statement and the Minister of Finance entered a denial to that also. The commissioner dealt with the evidence given by the hon. mfembei lor Halton and by Sir Edmund Osier, and I shall refer to that later on. I am sorry if I am taking too much of the time of the House, but it is impossible to lay the foundation of a case of this kind in order that the House may have an intelligent comprehension of all these circumstances without going fully into these matters.

I concede that
you require a great deal of time to lay the foundation for this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That may be, but the
foundation will be well and truly laid when I finish. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) proceeds:
Then he gives eight or ten cases where men had applied for small sums and had been put down for sums ten times as great, and where men who had subscribed nothing at all are put down on the stock list as actual subscribers. In all the instances so set forth in this writ, as I understand it, the names of these men are on the stock list which the Minister of Finance accepted on the sworn declaration of Travers, although comparison of the writ with the list would have given the plainest possible indication to the Minister of Finance not only of fraud in the first instance, but fraud persisted in up to and at the very time when this certificate was being asked for from the Government.
Then he goes on:
That Major Thomas Beattie, represented by the prospectus to have consented to act as a director, had not subscribed for any shares, and refused to be a director, and refused to allow his name to be used in any way in connection with bank, and the plaintiffs allege that the names of other persons were represented by the propectus to have consented to act as directors who had not subscribed for any shares or given any authority for any such publication.
Was it not open to the Minister of Finance to write a letter to Major Beattie and ask him whether that statement was true or false? Was it not competent also for the Minister of Finance to have taken the precaution which Major Beattie took to have looked up the record of Mr. Travers a little and to ascertain whether this matter was not worthy of further investigation by him. There is a further direct charge of fraud which ought to have
attracted the attention of the Minister of Finance in an especial manner.
Next he refers to the special endorsement upon the writs referred to in the communication from Mr. Leighton McCarthy. He states in reference to that:
The defendants in that suit under the terms of the settlement in court admitted in effect every one of the charges of fraud I have just now read.
Then he refers to Sir Edward Clouston's warning which only reached the Minister of Finance on November 30. Then he said:
I am not going into particulars of Sir Edward (Houston's warning just at this moment, but to be brief let me sum the whole situation in this way. The minister had the following warnings-in the first place he had the warning of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson). Again I repeat that, attributing equal sincerity to each, the testimony ot one who has a distinct recollection of a particular incident which impressed itself upon his memory, is always to be accepted against that of the other party who merely affirms that according to his recollection the incident did not occur. In the second place he had the warnings of other similar witnesses who can be produced if inquiry is granted. In the third place he had the warnings of Mr. Leighton McCarthy in the three letters referred to. In the fourth place he had the warnings contained in the writ of summons, and the endorsement. I want to point out to the minister and to the House that the charges in that writ were ot a two-fold nature, namely, those which concerned the plaintiff alone and those which concerned the public interest, and the duties of the Finance Minister. Among the latter were the charges that moneys had been illegally paid out by the provisional directors in contravention of the Bank Act, thus impairing the bank's capital.
Then, further on:
The written warning of the Canadian Bankers Association confirmed all previous warnings, and the Treasury Board should have instantly ordered the return of the certificate and failing compliance the Government should have peremptorily ordered the issue of a Royal Commission to investigate the alleged frauds. .	.
Then:
The Treasury Board had a plain and clear duty before it. We have been asked what could the Minister of Finance do? In the first place he could have ordered the production of the minute books, he should have ordered an investigation, he should have ordered further corroborative evidence, lie should not have granted that certificate after warnings which had been conveyed to him unless he was absolutely and positively assured by the evidence as to which there could be no doubt whatever that everything in connection with the Farmers Bank had been properly done in accordance with the law, and that no fraud was intended upon the Government of this country or upon the public. That is what he should have done. But, he says he was helpless when the direct and positive warning of Sir Edward Clouston came to him. I say he was far from help less.

He continued:
What should he have done? He should have sent a telegram after Travers. It is said that he sent a messenger after him, and that Travers refused to give up the certificate. That may be mere rumour; there may be nothing in it; and I do not vouch for it. But the minister should have sent a telegram after Travers ordering him to return that certificate immediately and telling him that if he failed to comply, the Government would the next day issue a Royal Commission to inquire into all the circumstances attending the organization of that bank and its application to the Treasury Board for a certificate. That is what the minister could have done, but that is what he did not do; and as the direct result of his inaction and neglect, the farmers of Canada, the workingmen of this country, have suffered losses to which they should not have been subjected.
There was no evidence to that effect given before the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
