speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The reason I am putting this on record is to show the views that were held at that time by the Prime Minister which afterwards caused him and the Government to issue a Royal Commission. He-states at this time that a Royal Commission should issue. I desire to read an extract from a speech of the present hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Hughes), as follows:
I support the motion of my hon. friend calling for a Royal Commission in order that there may be a full investigation into the affairs of the bank with the view of ascertaining, as has been said, where .these funds have been disposed of and how they have been disposed of and of ascertaining still further whether some of them may not be honestly and fairly reclaimed in order to lighten the burdens of the poor people who are the victims in this transaction. I support it also in order that evidence may be obtained which will be of great assistance to us in moulding the new Bank Act, and still further I support it on the ground that I am satisfied that if a Royal Commission is granted the matter will be brought home so closely to the Government and the negligence of the Government in issuing this certificate will be so clearly shown that the people concerned will have a just claim against the Government for the loss that they have sustained.
I desire to read-and this is the last quotation-an extract from the speech of the Hon-Mr. Crothers, now Minister of Labour, in the same debate. He said:

Now, I have no hesitation in making the charge, I believe the people of this country will make the charge, that the losses that the depositors and shareholders of the Farmers Bank have sustained are morally owing to the culpable negligence, the criminal negligence, of the Treasury Board. They made a mistake, to say the least of it; certainly they failed to exercise that common sense and that intelligence that any man would who had in his heart the best interests of the people of this country. And having got further evidence, he would have refused to authorize these people to open their doors and be in a position to bleed the public to the extent of millions-of dollars. I believe, therefore, it is the duty of Parliament to do something for these people. I do not know, I am not prepared to say, that they would have a legal claim against the Crown, because the Crown is supposed to do no wrong, by a monstrous fiction. But these people, having suffered this immense loss by reason of the negligence of the Treasury Board of this Government, this Government is morally responsible for the losses they have sustained, having taken the course they did.	[DOT]
I am reading that, not as evidence against the Treasury Board, but as indicating the view of a member of the present Government in 1911 on the assumption that there had been negligence. His view at that time was, and I have no doubt it is now, that if negligence could be shown on the part of the Treasury Board, and he alleged it at that time, that the Government would be morally responsible for the loss sustained by the depositors.

The commissioner
found against it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will come to that, and
we will see whether he found against it or not.
Nothing was done by the late Government in answer to the petition for relief from the depositors and shareholders in the bank. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has referred to the promise which he said was made by the present Prime Minister to the committee of shareholders and depositors as to his action in this matter, if returned to power. I have a copy of the communication which passed between Hon. Mr. Borden and the committee representing the depositors and the shareholders, during the summer of 1911 after the dissolution of the House and before the election, and I quote Mr. Borden's statement:
If returned to power we will make full inquiry by Royal Commission into circumstances connected with organization of Farmers Bank and granting certificate by Government. Our action with respect to depositors will be governed by result of inquiry.
I have tried to set forth fairly before the House the allegations and counter-allegations made by the parties in respect to thi3 matter. I have here the evidence containing the examination and cross-examination of Mr. Henderson and of Sir Edmund Osier, and of Mr. Fielding, but I would submit to the House that as it is substantially along the lines of the statements made bj these gentlemen in Parliament, it would be tedious and I think unnecessary that I should place it on ' Hansard.' I think I have placed the matter fairly before the House, showing the allegations made by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) in the House and in his evidence, and also by Sir Edmund Osier, and the denials entered by the Minister of Finance in the House.
After the present Government took office, further petitions were received on behalf of the shareholders and depositors for parliamentary relief, and the Government, in pursuance of the promise of the Prime Minister, appointed Sir William Meredith, now Chief Justice of Ontario, as a commissioner, with the following powers:
To make an investigation into all material and relevant facts in relation to:
(a)	The incorporation by Act of Parliament of the Farmers Bank of Canada and the organization thereof;
(b)	The application for and the giving by the Treasury Board of the certificate permitting the bank to issue notes and commence the business of banking;
(c)	The conduct and operation of the business of the bank, the amount of the capital subscribed and paid up, the causes of the suspension and failure, the extent of the liabilities and the value of the assets thereof.
Counsel were appointed by the Government and evidence was duly taken and the commissioner made his report in February, 1913. This report by Sir William Meredith and his findings are the basis for this legislation. It becomes necessary that I should examine Sir William Meredith's findings with some care, and particularly as to the circumstances surrounding the issue of the Treasury Board certificate. The commissioner says:
The application to the Treasury Board for the certificate was accompanied by what purported to be a list of the shareholders, and among other documents a statutory declaration of W. R. Travers, the general manager of the bank, in which he declares it is ' a list of the subscribers to the capital stock of the said bank correctly setting forth as to each subscription, the name of the subscriber, his address, the number of such shares subscribed by him, the amount of such shares and the amount paid in thereon ' and that each of the subscriptions ' is a bona fide subscription to the capital stock of the bank."

It will be necessary at this point to say a word as to Travers. The commissioner says he first appeared upon the scene in March, 1906. Travers, ias the House is aware, was the wrecker of the bank, and he is now serving a term in Kingston penitentiary. The commissioner says:
He appeared upon the scene first on March, 1906, when the provisional directors were endeavouring without success to obtain the necessary subscriptions to comply with the terms of the Bank Act as to obtaining a certificate for the commencement of business.
By an agreement entered into with him by the provisional directors by which he was authorized to sell the capital stock of the bank on the basis of a commission of 10 per cent. He was to be engaged as general manager, for five years at $4,000 for the first year, increasing by $1,000 in each of the four subsequent years, and after five years to receive a pension of $1,500 a year during his life.
So fhat we have an 'agreement entered into between the provisional directors and Travers, whereby he was to be general manager for ;a period of five years at ia salary stipulated and agreed upon. A subsequent agreement contains terms which it is not necessary to further mention. With respect to these agreements the Commissioner finds as follows:
It appears clear from these agreements and resolutions that what was intended was to sell the charter of the hank to Travers and to put him in control of its organization and business, and that the provisional directors should abdicate their functions and act in accordance with his directions, and that is what followed.
What is that from?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am reading from the report of the commissioner; and I shall, from this on, be dealing largely with the findings of that report and quoting from the report itself.
As I pointed out to the House, the provisions of the existing Bank Act require that $500,000 of the capital stock should he subscribed and that $250,000 should be paid thereon by the subscribers before the Treasury Board's certificate, necessary under the provisions of the Bank Act for the commencement of business could be issued. The finding of the commission upon that aspect of the case is as follows:
It is not open to question that $500,000 of the capital stock had not been then subscribed, and that $250,000 had not been paid by the subscribers.
There we have a positive and definite statement by the commissioner that the requirements of the Bank Act with respect

to the capital stock had not been complied with by the provisional directors of the board at the time the certificate Was issued. The commissioner finds further:
The statement in the declaration that the list of subscribers correctly set forth as each subscription ' the amount paid thereon ' and the statement that the $250,000 deposited to the credit of the Minister of Finance and the Receiver General was paid out of the moneys paid in and which actually had been received in respect of the shares, was literally true, but was calculated to deceive the Minister of Finance as to the real facts and was intended to do so.
Then he goes on to find:
The fact was that two sums amounting together to $100,000 had been borrowed by Travers from the Trust and Guarantee Company on the security of promissory notes made by applicants for shares which had been endorsed to him by the provisional directors for the express purpose of raising money to he used in making the deposit.
The commissioner then goes on to show the actions of Travers in respect of the application to the Treasury Board for the certificate.	He finds, with respect to
the raising of money upon these notes pledged to the Trust and Guarantee Company, as follows:
That in thus dealing with these notes the provisional directors and Travers were guilty of a breach of trust does not, I think, admit of doubt, and for the manner in which the money was borrowed and applied there was neither justification nor excuse.
He goes on then to find as follows with regard to the application to the Treasury Board for the issue of the required certificate :
My conclusion on this branch of the inquiry is that the Treasury Board was induced to give its certificate by false and fraudulent representations on the part of Travers, and that if the facts I have mentioned as to the way in which the $250,000 was made up had been disclosed, the certificate of the Treasury Board would not have been given.
The commissioner then refers to the verbal notice with which I dealt a little time ago, alleged to have been given by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) and Sir Edmund Osier, and this is his finding with regard to this alleged notice:
It is plain from the letter of the Finance Minister to Travers, of 30th November, 1906, that the Minister understood that section. 13 of the Bank Act would not have been complied with if the $250,000 was made up wholly or in part of money raised on promissory notes given by subscribers for shares to the provisional directors and that he would have felt it his duty to recommend that the certificate should not be granted if he had known that part of the money had been raised in that way.

That that information had been given to the minister before the certificate was issued appears from the testimony of Sir Edmond Osier and Mr. David Henderson and is shown by the letter of the 19th October, 1906, of Mr. Leighton McCarthy to the minister, which appears in exhibit 5, pp. 2, 3. In that letter Mr. McCarthy states as follows:
X have received information that the alleged subscribers for shares paid a large sum of money in cash and have signed notes for other large sums of money and that the persons professing to act in the name of the bank have transferred notes and received the proceeds and that a deposit either has been or will be made of the cash received and the proceeds of these notes or sufficient amount to make up $250,000.
That the verbal information I have mentioned was conveyed to Mr. Fielding was not denied though he stated that, as I have no doubt was the fact, no formal objection to the granting of the certificate was made either by Sir Edmund Osier or by Mr. Henderson. That, however, in my opinion is immaterial.
I call the attention of the House particularly to this finding of the commission that I now read:
I do not suggest that the minister would have been justified because of the information conveyed to him in recommending that the certificate should not be granted, or that the Treasury Board because of it would not have been justified in refusing to grant it, but, having received the information, it was in my opinion incumbent on the Treasury Board to have investigated the charges that had been made before coming to a conclusion as to whether or not the certificate should be given.

In connection with that,
would the minister read on page 6 of the commission's report towards the end of the page, the words beginning with ' The statement in the declaration that the list of subscribers? '

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I read that, but I will
read it again:
The statement in the declaration that the list of subscribers correctly set forth as each subscription ' the amount paid in thereon ' and the statement that the $250,000 deposited to the credit of the Minister of Finance and the Keceiver General was paid out of the moneys paid in and which actually had been received ir. respect of the shares, was literally true, but was calculated to deceive the Minister of Finance as to the real facts and was intended to do so.
Was literally true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I want the House to pay
particular attention to this finding of the commissioner:
I do not suggest that the minister would have been justified because of the information conveyed to him in recommending that the certificate should not be granted, or that the Treasury Board because of it would not have been justified in refusing to grant it, but, having received the information, it was in my opinion incumbent on the Treasury Board to
have investigated the charges that had been made before coming to a conclusion as to whether or not the certificate should be given.
He goes on to say:
The officials of the Department of Finance appear to have treated Mr. McCarthy's letter as if it had never existed, and, in my opinion, in that they erred, for although Mr. McCarthj on the 2nd November, 1906, wrote to the minister informing him that the claims made by his clients had been ' settled by their subscriptions being taken up by some parties interested in the bank and refunding the money paid by the individuals or returning the notes which had been given ' and had withdrawn the objections which he had made on behalf of his clients to the issue of the certificates, Mr. McCarthy did not in any way intimate that the information he conveyed to the minister as to the way in which the $250,000 had been made up had been found to be incorrect.
Will the minister permit a question? Is there any provision of law authorizing an investigation under oath before the Treasury Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot speak from memory as to the provisions of the Bank Act at that date, but I think the members of the Treasury Board might satisfy themselves in such manner as they deemed proper, by affidavits or otherwise. I am speaking from recollection.

When the commissioner speaks of an investigation, if he simply means making inquiries from subscribers in different parts of the country, it could hardly be expected that the Finance Department would do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend, who is a
lawyer, will observe that the commissioner finds that it was incumbent on the Treasury Board to have made an inquiry in view of the information which had been received by the minister.

The commissioner says
so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is his finding.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Such inquiry as would
satisfy them. If they had sent for the list of subscribers, or called for the minute book, if they had made an investigation, they would have discovered that the provisions of the Bank Act had not been complied with, that the provisional directors had abdicated their functions, as the commissioner says, in favour of Travers, that Travers was guilty of a breach of trust and was at that time a perjurer in making the statutory declaration,

and that he had been engaged for a period of five years to control the destinies of the bank as general manager.

If there is no legal
authority to make investigation, the department would be regarded as impertinent in making one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not agree with my
hon. friend that it would be regarded as impertinent, if positive information has come to the Treasury Board that there are grave irregularities. They should not fail to investigate the matter, call for the books of the bank, and for affidavits from others in connection with the application. 1 think they would discover any irregularity and would be able to justify themselves in withholding the certificate of the board necessary to the commencement of business.
The commissioner goes on:
It is true that, as Mr. Fielding stated in evidence, Travers, so far as he knew, was a reputable banker; but that was not, in my opinion, a sufficient reason for not having instituted an inquiry as to the matters which had been called to his attention. Such an inquiry could easily have been made, and the delay occasioned by it would have been inconsiderable, and such an inquiry would, undoubtedly, have resulted in the discovery of the manner in which the $100,000 had been raised and in the refusal of the Treasury Board to give the certificate.
This is a very important finding on the part of the commissioner. He says that, in his opinion, the fact that Travers was known to Mr. Fielding as a reputable banker was not a sufficient reason for not having instituted an inquiry as to matters which had been called to his attention. He says such an inquiry could easily have been made, and the delay occasioned by it would have been inconsiderable, and would have resulted in the discovery of the irregular manner in which the $100,000 had been raised, and in the refusal of' the Treasury Board to give a certificate. He says it was incumbent upon the Treasury Board to have prosecuted an inquiry in order to ascertain the facts, in view of the information which had been given. The commissioner then, after dealing with the facts connected with the issue of the certificate by the Treasury Board and making his findings thereon, goes on to deal with the conduct of the affairs of the hank subsequently, and I desire to put his findings in that connection upon 'Hansard.' He says:
Notwithstanding the irregularities on the part of Travers and his misconduct in connection with the application for the certificate, which

I have mentioned, the evidence satisfies me that if the bank had been prudently and honestly managed there is no reason why it should not have succeeded. The promissory notes that had been given by subscribers were for the most part good and were subsequently paid, and while it is true that if the certificate of the Treasury Board had not been granted the money of the shareholders and depositors would not have been lost, the efficient cause of that loss was the recklessness and fraud of those entrusted with the management of the bank, and not the granting of the certificate.
The efficient cause.
Has the minister been able to find out the meaning of the word 'efficient'?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In early days I examined many theories and authorities on the question of proximate and efficient causes -the causa causans of the old books. I would say that the efficient cause is the primary cause, without which loss, if loss is involved, would not have happened, notwithstanding that there may be some other contributory cause more immediately connected with the loss that subsequently occurred. I think I could find authority in support of that definition of efficient cause.
On what page is that statement made in the report?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On page 9 of the report of the commissioner, sessional paper 15.3a.
It will probably not be necessary for me to place upon 'Hansard' the finding of the commissioner with respect to the condition of the bank, as given in testimony before him by the liquidator. But, before coming to my argument, which will connect the finding of the commissioner more closely with the action of the Government, I desire to place upon 'Hansard' the finding of the commissioner with respect to the management of the affaire of the bank and the result of the administration of Travers. He says, on page 9 of the sessional paper in question:
The subsequent management of the affairs of the bank was characterized by gross extravagance, recklessness, incompetency, dishonesty and fraud, and has resulted in the entire loss of the paid-up capital and the whole of the deposits, and that after allowing for all that can be extracted from the shareholders on their double liability a loss amounting to no less than $1,806,437, making a record unparalleled in the history of any bank in Canada, or, as far as I am aware, In any other country.
Just in passing, I should like to call attention to the statement made by *the Prime Minister in the House on the last day of last session with regard to this

4G91
matter. He was asked a question by a member of the House, as follows:
Is it the intention of the Government to reimburse the depositors of the Farmers Bank? If so, does the Government propose to act in like manner with the depositors of the Bank of St. Jean and of the Bank Vile Marie?
The answer was as follows:
It appears from the report of the commissioner appointed to investigate the matter of the failure of the Farmers Bank (a) That the issue of the certificate of the Treasury Board authorizing the bank to commence business, was procured by false and fraudulent representations on the part of the promotor and subsequent general manager of the bank, W. B. Travers. (b) That in the commissioner's opinion it was incumbent upon the Treasury Board before issuing its certificate, to have investigated certain charges made to the Department of Finance that the amount required by the Bank Act to be paid in respect of subscriptions, had not in fact been so paid, and (c) That if the true facts had been disclosed, the certificate of the Treasury Board would not have been given, and thus the bank under the management of Travers would not have been authorized to commence business.
The case is of exceptional and indeed unique character, both with regard to the fraudulent means by which the certificate was procured and in respect of the results which followed, involving the ultimate loss of all moneys placed in the bank by the unfortunate depositors. The man who fraudulently procured the certificate in the name of the bank, was enabled to attract those deposits by the unwarranted assumption of powers in violation of plain statutory conditions. While the direct subsequent cause of the loss was the fraud and dishonestly of the banks' manager in the administration of its affairs, there is nevertheless a certain connection between that loss and the power and status with which he became invested upon the granting of the certificate. Having regard to these considerations, the Government consider that the depositors are entitled to a reasonable measure of relief, which will be provided by legislation to be introduced at the next session of Parliament.
The case of the other banks mentioned, is m no wise similar, and the action which the Government propose to take in the case of the Farmers Bank will afford no warrant or precedent for reimbursing their depositors.
What is the justification for the measure of legislative relief which we are bringing down in the matter of the Farmers'* Bank and its depositors? I have called the attention of the House to the finding of the commissioner as to the duty of the Treasury Board in view of the information which had been received from Mr. McCarthy, from the hon. member for Halton and from the hon. member for West Toronto. Let me repeat it. The commissioner finds that:
It was incumbent on the Treasury Board to have investigated . the charges that had been
made before coming to a conclusion as to whether or not a certificate should be given.
The House is aware that such investigation was not made. A certificate was issued, the Treasury Board not having made the inquiry which the commissioner finds it was their duty to have made. Failure on the part of' an individual or a public body to discharge a duty which is incumbent upon him or it is negligence at common law. The finding of the commissioner, therefore, is that the Treasury Board was negligent in not having investigated the .charges which 'had been made before coming to a conclusion as to whether or not the certificate should be given. I submit that that cannot be controverted; that if it was incumbent upon them to do something which they did not do, they were negligent. If the charges had been investigated by the Treasury Board in pursuance of its duty as found by the commissioner, the following would have been disclosed:
1.	The agreement which Travers had with the provisional directors under which, in the words of the commissioner, Travers was put in control of the organization and business of the bank, the provisional directors abdicating their functions and agreeing to act in accordance with his directions.
2.	That Travers was to be general manager of the bank for five years.
3.	That the meeting of subscribers had teen irregularly called.
4.	That the amount required by the Bank Act to be paid by the subscribers had not been paid.
5.	That Travers had been guilty of a breach of trust, as found by the commissioner.
6.	That Travers had made a false declaration and had attempted to deceive the minister -and the board.
I say that if the Treasury Board had made the investigation which it was incumbent upon them to have made in pursuance of their duty, these facts would have been disclosed. I ask the House whether, if the facts had been disclosed, the Treasury Board certificate would have been granted, or, if subsequently granted, the bank would have been enabled to commence business with Travers as its general manager? I submit that the Treasury Board certificate would not have been issued; at all events it would not have been issued at that time and if it had

Does the minister not
think, then,' that subscribers for stock after the certificate had been issued should be placed in exactly the same position as the depositors?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I explained the other
day when wTe were discussing the resolution which preceded this Bill that it is entirely out of the question for the Government, following any logical method of

dealing with this matter, to relieve the shareholders.

To relieve the shareholders who subscribed prior to the issue of the certificate, but if the Government feels that the depositors must be paid on account of the negligence of the Treasury Board, why not pay the subscribers for stock after the certificate of the Treasury Board was issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Because the subscribers
to stock, as soon as the stock is allotted to them, become shareholders; the shareholders elect directors to manage the bank and the directors select and continue m office a general manager. There is no question that the directors are the agents of the shareholders, and the general manager is the official of the directors. The shareholders are the proprietors of the bank. I do not know upon what basis the Government could come to the relief of the shareholders, the actual proprietors of the bank whose agents, the directors, had continued Travers in office and to some extent participated in the reckless management of the bank. The commissioner makes the point that if the bank had been honestly managed there would have been no loss.
I say that if Travers had not been the general manager the bank would probably have succeeded; on the law of probabilities it would have succeeded. The failure, therefore, of the Farmers Bank followed upon the negligence of the Treasury Board in failing to investigate that which the commissioner says dt was incumbent on them to investigate. The general argument would go something like this:	No certificate, no bank, no bank, no loss; or if the bank had been permitted subsequently to open for business then; if no Travers in charge, no loss. So that in both cases we get back to the negligent action on the part of the Treasury Board in granting a certificate without making investigations which it was their plain duty to have made. The certificate of the Treasury Board empowered the bank, with Travers at its head, to invite deposits and to enter upon the career of misconduct which brought ruin to thousands of the depositors.
I may say in concluding my remarks that the Government feels that it is morally bound to make reparation, and we have been unable to see on any logical ground that anything short of the full amount- of the loss -can be fairly offered to

these depositors who have suffered, aa I have shown, through the negligence of the Treasury Board in granting the certificate. I have placed upon ' Hansard ' previously the position of the liquidation as given to me in a statement by the liquidators, so it will be unnecessary to refer to that further. The Bill authorizes payment to depositors of the full amount of their losses, and the Government in respect of any moneys paid to them will be subrogated to their rights. So far as I can see from the statement given by the liquidators, all the assets of the bank will be required to meet the charges of liquidation and the preferred claims, so that I do not think the subrogation to the rights of the depositors will result in the Government receiving any of the proceeds of the liquidation.
I beg, therefore, to move the second reading of the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to conclude my remarks upon the second reading of the Bill this evening, and therefore I shall abandon some aspects of the discussion which I proposed taking up had the remarks of the Minister of Finance been delivered to the House earlier in the day.	.
I cannot but feel, and I trust I say so truthfully, that every hon. gentleman in the House must be impressed with the fact that the Minister of Finance himself felt he was presenting to the House very doubtful legislation indeed for our enactment. The Minister of Finance says that the Government feel themselves under a moral obligation to repay losses sustained toy the depositors in the Farmers Bank. He asserted that they realised the existence of this moral obligation three years ago. I have only to say, this moral obligation did not press heavily upon the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance or the members of the Government or they would not have allowed three years to elapse without moving in the matter. Under the provisions of the Bank Act, the Farmers Bank was chartered in 1904, I think. The bank was not organized under the charter originally granted in 1904; it was renewed in 1905, and again in 1906. It eventually received a certificate from the Treasury Board enabling it to commence business. In 1910 the Farmers Bank failed with liabilities to depositors aggregating $1,000,-
000.	In 1911 or 1912 the present Government appointed a Royal Commission to inquire into the circumstances attending the issuance of this certificate and the facts attending the 296
failure of this bank. That commissioner found that the failure of that bank was due to fraudulent and incompetent management, and I say that was the obvious, logical and truthful finding.
The Bill before us is a measure to enable the Government to repay the depositors of the Farmers Bank the losses sustained by them, and the question before hon. members is whether or not they will support the measure. I submit that, in all the reasons submitted by the Minister of Finance, there is not sufficient to justify him in asking us to support this legislation. The Minister of Finance was particularly weak when he appealed to ' Hansard ' and read statements made by members of Parliament in 1911, when the matter of the issuance of the certificate to the Farmers Bank was a subject of debate, in a session preceding a general election, when party feeling was running high. I say I was surprised at the Minister of Finance presenting extracts from these debates on this occasion. I believe that there are members in this House to-day who spoke in 1911 upon the motion to which the minister referred and who to-day do not believe in the views they then expressed. It is said further that in the Senate there are one or two members who were then members of this House of Commons and who spoke upon the very motion to which the Minister of Finance referred, who to-day are canvassing their fellow members in the Senate against supporting this measure, notwithstanding the fact that in 1911 they spoke favourably to the motion which was referred to by the Minister of Finance.
Name, name.
I am not going to give the names. If hon. gentlemen want to know the names I will give them privately.
Names, names.

Unless there exist
stronger reasons in justification of this proposed legislation than the contradictory statements of the hon. member for Halton, the hon. member for West Toronto, and Mr. Fielding, the late Minister of Finance, the legislation should be withdrawn. Let me repeat what I said on a former occasion during the present session that I regard this legislation as extremely unfortunate. It is extremely difficult to understand why the Government should present it. Do they really believe in it. I doubt if hon. members sitting behind the Government will be



enthusiastic in casting their votes in support of this measure. I doubt if the Government, among their own political friends in or out of this House, will find any substantial encouragement for pressing this legislation upon Parliament. If the Government believed that a moral obligation rested upon them to recoup depositors of the Farmers Bank, the legislation would have been submitted to us long before the dying days of the third session of this Parliament. It is pretty generally and publicly admitted that this legislation is unjustified, and I would have been glad if the minister had said to his supporters: The Bill simply represents the views of the executive, it is not presented as a Government measure, and Government supporters are at liberty to exercise freely their best judgment and vote as they see fit.
While opposing this Bill, I cannot resist expressing my regret for the loss sustained by the depositors in the Farmers Bank. I suppose that every hon. member on this side of the House will join with me in this expression of regret. It was a disastrous failure. It brought some men to premature graves. Some were placed in the prisons of this country. To others came unexpectedly want and sorrow, and to all those who have suffered in these and other ways I am sure that we all join in expressing our regret for this unfortunate disaster. But we must deal with a measure of this kind in a business-like way, lest we establish a precedent which the country would in the future very much regret. The Farmers Bank was started in November, 1904, by an Act of this Parliament. The bank did not organize under its original Act of incorporation, but by the further Acts of Parliament the charter was extended in 1905 and 1906. The provisions of the Bank Act require that any bank started by Act of Parliament must organize within a year; otherwise its charter lapses. A serious obligation rests upon Parliament when it undertakes to grant a
11 p.m. charter to any number of gentle-ment to organize a bank. The responsibility for the organization, and for all the events in connection with the Farmers Bank subsequent to the incorporation down to its failure is more directly attributable to the act of Parliament than it is to any ministerial act of the Department of Finance. It is an undoubted fact that the then Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) was opposed openly to the granting of a charter to the applicants for a bank to be known as the Farmers Bank.

He divined apparently the trouble which ensued. He was rather prejudiced against the name that the incorporators were seeking for this bank. He thought the promoters were likely to secure as shareholders for this bank a class of people who were little accustomed to banking or commercial transactions, and he so expressed this opinion in the Banking and Commerce Committee. I want to point out to the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), who became a very brave and outspoken man after disaster had overtaken this bank, that if he had shown the same amount of courage and interest in his constituents who were probable subscribers to the stock of the Farmers Bank on the occasion when the promoters were seeking a charter, and had opposed the granting of this charter, he would have done his duty to a greater degree than he did.

On what ground

The hon. gentleman
might at least have opposed the granting of the name ' Farmers Bank.' He knew that the Minister of Finance was opposed to granting them that name. He told the Minister of Finance privately that they should not have obtained the name, and his only excuse was that he was afraid of his constituents and consequently would not undertake to oppose it in the committee.

Where is your
authority for that?

The evidence of the
late Minister of Finance, I trust I may say to the hon. member for Halton that in the discussion of this matter, he will not seek refuge under any of the rules of the House of Commons, when we on this side of the House do not see our way clear to accept his statement of some of the facts in issue in this matter.
I have not done so.

I want to say to the hon. member for Halton that I trust he will not; and I do not think he should. With all due deference to the hon. gentleman, I do not think his conduct in connection with the Farmers' .Bank, as a friend of its depositors is one of which he may feel particularly proud. _
I was remarking that the late Minister of Finance was opposed to the granting to the incorporators of the name ' Farmers'

Bank ' and I think he was justified. He anticipated that the granting of this name to the proposed bank would deceive a certain class of the public and might possibly, as it did, cause a great deal of trouble. When Parliament undertakes to grant a charter to certain named persons to engage in the banking business, Parliament is responsible for the creation of the institution. The conditions which an incorporated and organized bank, is required to comply with before the certificate ' is issued are purely formal, and I do not think that failure to comply absolutely with these requirements is a very serious matter, the important matter being the granting of the charter by Parliament. The charter enables the incorporators to solicit subscriptions, to receive payment upon stock subscriptions, to pay into the hands of the Receiver General the $250,000 required by the Act, to select their directors, and in fact it practically enables them to organize the bank and do everything except issue notes. The purpose of requiring the incorporators to obtain from the Treasury Board a certificate before commencing business was to protect the public against the premature issuance of notes. When the Farmers Bank was chartered by Parliament, that charter enabled the stockholders to organize their bank, to elect their directors, and to do everything necessary in respect to the carrying on of a general banking business, except the right of note-issue, and when they obtained the certificate from the Treasury Board they were entitled to make a note issue up to the amount of their unimpaired paid-up capital.
It is argued that the requirements of the Bank Act were not strictly complied with before the certificate was issued, and that this certificate was obtained from the Trea-[DOT] sury Board fraudulently and through deception. I do not intend to argue against the finding of the commissioner in this respect. He finds that this certificate was obtained by fraud and by deception. It is not necessary to argue against it nor does it follow that if the finding of the commissioner in that respect is correct that this legislation is justified. I see little relevancy between the findings of the commissioner and the measure now before us. The Minister of Finance does not look to the vital and essential particulars of the findings of the commissioner to justify his legislation. Under the Bank Act stock subscription to the amount of $500,000 is required before the certificate of the Treasury Board can be issued.

It is very questionable, indeed, whether or not the bank fulfilled this particular condition. I would like to call to the attention of the House the finding of the commissioner on that point, and then I think hon. gentlemen will see that there was no very substantial neglect or failure to comply with the requirements of the Bank Act, so far as the amount of stock subscription was concerned. The report says:
It was contended that the statement in the statutory declaration of Travers, made on the 27th November, 190G, to which I have referred, and a copy of which appears on pages 7 and 8 of the return (exhibit 5), that the list of subscribers marked exhibit D to the declaration correctly set forth as to each subscription the name of the subscriber, his address, the number of shares subscribed by him and the amount of his shares, and that each subscription was a bona fide subscription to the capital stock of the bank, was untrue. The number of shares subscribed for, as shown by the list, was '5,792, though by an error in the addition it was stated to be 5,789, and the amount subscribed was $579,200, a corresponding error as to this having been made in adding up the figures; of these shares it was, however, stated that 35 were subscribed after the 22nd October, 1906, which as I have mentioned was the date of the first publication in the Globe newspaper of the notice calling the meeting of the subscribers, and Travers appears to have thought that subscriptions received down to and including that day, but not those received after it, were to be taken into account in making up the $50,000 which section 13 of the Bank Act requires to be bona fide subscribed before the meeting of the subscribers is called.
In substance, the commissioner finds that prior to the day upon which appeared for the first time, the notice published by the directors calling the first meeting of shareholders, there was not $500,000 of stock actually subscribed. But if you take into consideration' subscriptions' which were received up to the date of the first appearance in the Globe newspaper of the notice calling together the meeting of the shareholders to elect directors, then $500,000 worth of stock was subscribed, and the commissioner finds that Mr. Travers thought he was justified in including the amount of stock subscribed down to that date. The commissioner proceeds:
If the 22nd October, 1906, be the determining date, and as I think allotment was necessary to constitute an applicant for shares a subscriber within the meaning of the Act, the statement as to the number of shares that had been bona fide subscribed for was untrue, and on the hypothesis I have just mentioned less than 5,000 shares had been subscribed for.
Even if you take this view as given by the commissioner in the paragraph I have just read, there was a very slight deficit in the amount of capital required

to be subscribed before calling the general meeting of shareholders for the election of directors. The commissioner proceeds:
If, however, all the shares for which bona
fide application had been then made were properly included, or the determining date was the date of the meeting of the subscribers, the statement was true.
At any rate we have the finding by the commissioner that there was $500,000 of the Farmers' Bank stock subscribed up to the day on which appeared in a newspaper published in the city of Toronto the first notice calling the shareholders together for organization purposes and for the purpose of electing directors. It is true that the Bank Act requires that, before this meeting shall be called, that amount of stock must be subscribed. There is no definite finding of the commissioner therefore that there was not $500,000 of stock properly subscribed within the terms and provisions of the Bank Act. But admitting that there was a shortage in the amount of stock subscribed at this time, I say that the deficiency was very slight indeed and not important in its consequences. Mr. Travers, I think, honestly believed that the statement he made to the Treasury Board in this respect was perfectly correct, and that he was justified in making it; and the error, if any, was so small and inconsequential that I think it affords a very poor and weak foundation upon which to rear the legislation we are now discussing.
The charge is also made that the $250,000 in cash, which the Bank Act requires shall be bona fide paid by stock subscribers before the calling of the first meeting of shareholders, was not bona fide paid. I think the finding of the commissioner is at least to that effect, and I am not going to argue that the evidence presented to the commissioner would justify any other finding. But there is this to be said, that a very considerable proportion of the $250,000 had been actually paid in by stock subscribers; that Mr. Travers had secured from the provisional directors, whether properly or not, a power of attorney empowering him to endorce notes received by the provisional directors in payment of stock subscriptions. The preliminary expenses in connection with the organization of the bank were excessive, the amount exceeding $40,000. When Mr. Travers required the $250,000 to deposit with his application for the certificate, he was considerably short. He resorted to the method of endorsing stock-subscribers' notes to the amount of over $100,000 to the Trust and Guarantee Company of the city of Toronto, upon which
[Mr. A. K. Manias* o.I
security he borrowed from this company $80,000. With this $80,000 and $20,000 additional borrowed from the same company upon other collateral he secured his $250,000. It is only fair to point out to the House that Mr. Travers at the moment did not adopt this method of procuring this $250,000 in any secret manner. He thought in so doing he was within his legal rights. This further should be said, that Mr. Travers, having been for a long number of years engaged in the banking business, had a considerable knowledge of what had been the practice in this respect by banks in similar circumstances. It is generally accepted as a fact that frequently subscribers' notes have been discounted to secure the amount for deposit with the Receiver General. I suppose Mr. Travers was well acquainted with this practice, and thought he might safely imitate a practice well known in the country. It is perhaps well that we inquire at this stage what is the purport of requiring a deposit of $250,000 with the Receiver General prior to application for the Treasury Board certificate. This was not always the law in Canada. Prior to 1890 a payment of only $100,000 upon the subscribed capital of a bank was required. There was a further provision that a second $100,000 would have to be paid within a certain time, I think two years, after commencing to do business, and the purpose in increasing that amount from $200,000 to $250,000 was not intended for the protection particularly of depositors or creditors, but for the purpose of encouraging the organization of banks with large capital in this country. That was the reason assigned by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce in 1890 in presenting to Parliament for revision the Bank Act.
It seems clear to me, and to anybody approaching this question in an unbiased fashion, that the failure of the Farmers' Bank in a small degree to comply with the actual requirements of the Bank Act, in respect of the amount of capital required to be subscribed, and the actual amount of bona fide payments to be made upon stock subscriptions prior to the application for the treasury certificate, was, after all, not a very substantial one; and that failure was by no means the cause of the subsequent failure of the bank.

recklessness and speculation on the part of the manager?

I do not think so; I wouid not think that that would be a fair deduction. In some cases the result might be as suggested by the hon. member, but I do not think it would he necessarily due to the fact that the bank was starting with an amount of capital less than that required by the Bank Act.
Did it not have that effect ' directly in this case?

It has been urged, Mr. Speaker, that the department did not exercise the necessary caution and supervision of the representations or allegations made on behalf of the bank by Mr. Travers when making his application for the certificate, and that, it is owing to this failure to make a very careful supervision of the statements made to the Treasury Board that the failure of the bank ensued. I take this ground in respect to this contention, that it was not the proximate or effective cause of the bank failure. That is the finding of the commissioner. The depositors, I say, did not extend credit to the bank upon the ground that it had or had not the Government certificate. The people of Canada know that there is no Government guarantee against loss by a bank's operations except as to note issue. I say that the Government can produce no depositor of the late Farmers' Bank who will say that he or she was induced to make a deposit owing to the fact that the bank received the certificate from the Treasury Board. Their mind was not influenced one way or the other by this fact.
Let us see what was the scope of the reference to the commissioner in respect of the Farmers Bank. It was read by the Minister of Finance and consequently I need not read it at length. But one of the matters which the commissioner was directed to investigate was the conduct and operation of the business of the bank, the amount of capital subscribed and paid up, the causes of the suspension and failure, and the extent of the liabilities, and the value of the assets thereon. It has long been established that the man who deposits money in a bank is, in his relation to that bank, a lender of money, and the bank is a borrower. In the event of failure the depositor will always be considered a voluntary creditor. It was never the purpose of the Canadian banking laws to guarantee depositors in our banks against loss. That idea was suggested in the Committee on Banking and Commerce last year when it had under consideration the revision of the Bank Act and the suggestion received very little if any support from members of that committee. I most emphatically

I do not know what

He never did.

That statement was
made in this House on more than one occasion and was never denied. It is a very probable thing that the Minister of Labour would make that statement during the election of 1911, because he had made practically the same statement in this House in 1911.
I make the contradiction most emphatically.

Of the statement that the Conservative party made promises in my constituency to reimburse the losses in the Farmers Bank.

I am sorry I cannot accept the statement of the hon. gentleman, but I trust he will not think that I am disrespectful to him when I decline to accept his statement upon this point.
I say that the Conservative party, for the purpose of electing candidates in certain constituencies in the province of Ontario, promised repayment of losses to the depositors in the Farmers Bank; that these statements were made for that purpose and to accomplish that end. If the Conservative party really were sincere in making these promises during the election of 1911, they should have long since implemented their promises*, instead of postponing this measure until this very late date. In expressing my opposition to this Bill, which I have done, in a very discursive way and incompletely, I think I am voicing public opinion. I believe it is the opinion of all members that legislation of this kind should Inever have been introduced. The country will agree with me when I say that this legislation is before us merely because it is pressed upon the Government by a few hon. gentlemen in this House who found their way here by reason of the support which they obtained in the last general election on account of their promise to secure repayment from the Government to de-

positors of any losses which they might have incurred.
Is that the reason why the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) is supporting this Bill?

I really do not know.
That is the view of the people; that opinion is expressed in a great number of newspapers ordinarily favourable and sympathetic to the Conservative party and the present ministry. There is nothing in law or in equity to justify this legislation. There is nothing in any of the facts disclosed in the proceedings of the Royal Commission to justify the conclusions made by the Minister of Finance upon which he bases this measure. It is unfortunate legislation in every respect; it presents to Parliament a very pernicious and unfortunate precedent which this country will in the future regret if we pass this legislation, and I think this House should not express its adherence to the principle of the Bill. Therefore I beg to move:
That the word 'now' be struck out and the words 'this day six months' be added at the end of the motion.

Only recently a prominent justice of the Superior Court of Ontario, Sir William Meredith, was appointed a commissioner to conduct an inquiry into the Farmers Bank, an inquiry which I said speaking a few days ago, was both useless and mischievous.

With regard to his aspersions against the hon. member for Hal ton, I would like to tell the hon. gentleman that members on this side, and I believe members on that side, except himself, have the highest regard for the hon, member for Halton for his word, his probity of conduct and his worthy actions from the beginning of his career up to the present moment. It little works then to the advantage of the hon member for Halifax, to argue in this fashion for partisan purposes, and to weaken the evidence that the hon. member for Halton gave, knowing that it tells against his own party affiliations and that it was a damaging bit of evidence that he had to overcome. I was surprised, Mr. Speaker, to see the hon. gentleman, who is usually fair, and who keeps to high standards, descend to make what was a personal and threatening attack -against the hon. member for H-altom for the unmagnaaimous purpose of attempting to -make political capital at the expense of as honourable a gentleman as there ever was in this House. Is the level of debate to be dragged down by mem holding high places like the hon. member, who for some party purpose, cannot discuss -a question on its merits without attacking hon. gentlemen on this side? I hope that the hon. gentlem-an has not been inspired to attack the hon. member for Halton; I fear it was lack of preparation, because he -admits himself he laboured, and to be as charitable -as I can I will say, that not having much to say he fell down eggregiously, -and made a mistake in attacking -a gentleman of the standing enjoyed by the hon. member for Halton.
The junior member for Halifax said that the Government seemed to be hard pressed, that they had waited for three years to carry

out the measures of relief after they obtained power; and in the same breath he complains that they are doing it even now. There is an old saying that it is better late than never; but you cannot satisfy the hon. gentleman. He complains:	They did not
do it soon enough, he now complains that they are doing it too late, a futile argument, purely partisan, absolutely without anything to base it on, and an argument that is not worthy of the mental attainments of the hon. gentleman. He says that the situation is one that is not only vicious but mischievous. What is the position? Has the hon. gentleman no constituents for whom he speaks? Was there a Farmers Bank in his constituency; had he one of the twenty-seven or twenty-eight banks that failed? The hon. gentleman has some colleagues who have spoken on this subject and who have supported the proposition that the Government should relieve the depositors. I can understand the argument of the hon. gentleman when he attempts to convince the House that this ought to be a question upon which there should be no party vote, one that should not have been introduced by the Government, a question which his two colleagues who have hundreds of sufferers could vote for, and he could vote against. But the Government in this case have taken a courageous stand, and, being a money measure, I presume they must introduce it. The Bill is based upon what the Prime Minister said before he brought this legislation down, and after a fair discussion of the Bill, if it receives a majority in this House, no matter whether the majority is on that side or on this side, it will become law if it receives a majority.
The hon. member remarked that the Senate has been lobbied by gentlemen in this House who spoke in favour of this Bill. I know nothing about that. But, Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman's friends are in control of the Senate, and I have yet to learn that Conservatives in the Senate have influence sufficient to make the majority bow to the will of the minority. I do not like the argument. I fear my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax has something up his sleeve; he knows something about his own friends in the Senate.
No, you would like to see the Senate defeat it.
I said that the hon. gentleman's friends-

Your friends.
[Mr. Morphy.}
My friends in this House would like to see the Senate defeat it. Is that what the hon. gentleman means?
A great many of them.

I will attend to that
argument a little later on, and show where we stand from the point of view of the representatives of the people. I represent a county that has been severely struck in two ways. I will give the details later. But I first want to refer to the statement of the Prime Minister in this House which has been put on record to-night by the Minister of Finance wherein he promised on the 6th of June, 1913, that he would introduce legislation to relieve these unfortunate depositors. It is late, and I am going to endeavour to cut my remarks short. I will not give again what the Minister of Finance quoted to-night. But the statement of the Prime Minister was clean-cut, unequivocal, and absolute last year that he would introduce this Bill this year; and it is before us. He made use of the language a part of which I quote:
The case is of exceptional and indeed of unique character both with regard to the fraudulent means by which this certificate was produced and in respect of the results which followed, involving the ultimate loss of all moneys placed in the bank by the unfortunate depositors.
The man who fraudulently procured the certificate in the name of the Dank was enabled to attract those deposits by the unwarranted assumption of powers in violation of plain statutory conditions. While the direct subsequent cause of the loss was the fraud and dishonesty of the bank's manager in the administration of its affairs, there is nevertheless a certain connection between that loss and the power and status with which he became invested upon the granting of the certificate. Having regard to these considerations, the Government consider that the depositors are entitled to a reasonable measure of relief, which will be provided by legislation to be introduced at the next session of Parliament.
Implementing these remarks, the Finance Minister introduced the following resolution :	>
That it is expedient to provide that there may be paid and applied from and out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada, a sum not exceeding in the whole one million two hundred thousand dollars to pay to persons who were creditors for money on deposit in the Farmers Bank of Canada, the respective amounts standing at their credit in the books of the bank when the bank suspended payment.
Upon that resolution a Bill has been introduced. Let us see how the failure of this bank has affected the people. According to the returns brought down, the taxes collected on the 14th of December, 1906, the

year of failure, in certain municipalities were deposited in the Farmers Bank. In the municipality of West Zorra, the taxes collected from the people and deposited in the Farmers Bank amounted to J18.741.07; Camden East, $15,115.19; Mornington, m the county which I represent, $10,674.96; Scott, $64,485,91; Esquesing, $4,448.59; township of Kerwood, $3,747.24; Brucefield, $6,347.13; Embro, $5,566.73. This means that the losses in this respect struck every man, woman and child in these municipalities. These taxes were collected on December 14, five days before the bank failed, and were deposited not for speculation but for safe keeping in a Canadian bank to which a charter had been granted by this Parliament. In the township of Mornington, 2,746 people are direct losers in connection with these taxes. The losses in the other townships would average about the same; I have not taken the trouble to figure them up. In the township of Mornington in my county 304 persons were depositors in this bank, Liberals and Conservatives, without distinction of political affiliation. Does my hon. friend object to the Liberals of that county receiving money that has been stolen from them through this failure merely for the sake of the principle in respect of which he takes such a lofty stand ?
I do not believe that any money was stolen.
The hon. gentleman makes no distinction between Liberals and Conservatives in this matter ?
Certainly not.

He is opposed to any one being remunerated in this regard. I hope that as the representative of North Perth 1 will never seek to make any capital out of a matter of this kind. I hope that the time will never come when the unfortunate people of whom the hon. member for Halifax spoke so feelingly to-night and with whom there was connected death, suicide, broken hearts, asylums and disaster, will be made by me the subject of political capital. I hope the day will never come when I shall attempt to make political capital out of the misfortunes of any class of people, whether I represent them or not. I think it is descending pretty low in the scale when a tremendous loss of this kind is debated with a heat that is devoid of all sympathy for the unfortunate ones.
Do not think that there are any politics in my views; there may be in your own, but there are not in mine. I am not in a position to be prejudiced.

On February 12, 1912, a Royal Commission was issued to Sir William Meredith to make investigation. Very wide powers were given to him under this commission; they have been related by the Minister of Finance, and I need not repeat them. The commissioner made his return, sessional paper 153a. It is concise and easily understood. I desire to specify for the better understanding of my argument certain dates connected with this matter. On November 30,	1906, at a
meeting of the Treasury Board, the issue of the certificate to commence business was authorized, and the certificate was issued on that day. Two months later, on January 2, 1907, the bank began business. Three years and eleven months later, on December 19, 1910, the bank suspended payment. The failure of the bank, which had twenty-six or twenty-eight branches in Ontario, affected thousands of depositors who were conducting savings or current accounts and who were distributed over widely separated sections of the province. These depositors petitioned the Government of Canada for relief, and the main ground of their application was that the Treasury Board of this country, a board established for the careful consideration, amongst other things, of the issue to banks of certificates to do business after being incorporated, was guilty of negligence in connection with the issue of the certificate under which the Farmers' Bank was launched as a public institution. The general manager, Mr. Travers, who has been spoken of in terms which I shall not repeat, was handed a certificate impressed with the seal and approval of the Dominion Government and sent into the public market to get public business, particularly from the farmers, under circumstances which led only to one end, disaster. Nothing else could be hoped for; it was a case of disaster, loss and ruin to those who had dealings with the concern at the head of which was Mr. Travers. It is argued that the Treasury Board was culpable and guilty of negligence in the issue of that certificate, and that through that negligence the people have suffered. It has been truly said by the Minister of Finance, that if there had been no certificate issued there would have been no bank; if no bank, no deposit; if no deposits no loss. From that point of view it is unnecessary to consider with any hair-splitting, narrow arguments from the lawyer's point of view or otherwise, what the proximate cause of the loss was or what was the efficient cause

of the loss. If I may be permitted to use another word, I should like to say that we should consider what was the deficient cause of the loss, the defective action on the part of the Treasury Board that caused the loss. That is coming closer to the point. There was no efficiency about it. The whole situation and the action of the Treasury Board is reeking with deficiency, with defective operation, with no operation; with neglect, with failure to act. That is the most startling thing about the whole situation from the Treasury Board's point of view.
What is the good of talking about the law in a case of this kind? Parliament can make the law. What is the good of talking about politics? The people will make the politics. They will attend to those who do wrong and those who do right; and I advise the hon. gentlemen to get in and come with us if they feel that way and make this thing unanimous in favour of those who have suffered. No one here desires to take any glory out of this. Let us see if there is not something in the case that can be treated from an equitable and conscientious point of view, mot from a legal hair-splitting point of view, as to whether there has been efficient or proximate cause and what the causes were. The point is that the depositors make their application and they make it upon a basis that is sufficient to arouse in the minds of any reasonable man in this House feelings which would compel him to approach the subject from a point of view of equity and good conscience nather than of the fine hair-splitting points of law. This country, as was said by the leader of the Opposition, ought to be big enough and fair enough to do what is right in this or any other ease. That is the ground on which I would like to see it put, and on which it should be put. The Parliament of this country have been decent in lots of cases where they had less right or reason to go out of their way to do the decent thing than in this case. If an equitable claim exists to such an extent that it ought to move this Parliament, then Parliament can make the laws to suit its case. That is the intention of the resolution before this House. The Minister of Finance introduced the resolution into this House in the most courteous, careful, studied manner so as not to create offence. He laid himself open to arguments which were seized upon by the press 
of this country who proclaimed far and wide that the minister had made the admission that the Finance Minister ox the Treasury Board in the preceding Government had not been guilty of negligence but only of an error of judgment and that therefore the whole thing fell down on the admission, of the Minister of Finance. That was making politics with a vengeance.

Is that not what it
was?
I do not intend to reply to that from any hon. gentleman who has ever sat upon the Bench. That question is unworthy of the hon. gentleman who asked it.
